Downstream estimation, planning, and spatial memory require structured measurements: metric positions, bounding volumes, and semantic classes, with directly measured velocity where the sensing modality supplies it. Translating raw streams into those measurements is the perception pipeline's responsibility. Whatever form its output takes, whether an explicit message packet or an observation token sequence, it must carry three mandatory properties before any consumer can use it: a capture timestamp, a reference frame, and a qualified uncertainty envelope.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Sense node."}
*The Sense stage: photons become dated, framed claims.*
:::

The first mandatory property is the **capture timestamp**\index{Capture timestamp!definition} ${\CaptureTimestamp}_0$, which specifies the temporal midpoint of the energy integration window, the effective instant of a camera exposure or a laser firing. Physical sensors do not take instantaneous snapshots. An optical camera integrates photons across an exposure duration, and a mechanical lidar sweeps laser pulses over an azimuth arc across several milliseconds. Downstream state observers and vision-language-action policies require ${\CaptureTimestamp}_0$ to ground observation tokens into the machine's dynamic equations of motion. By contrast, the arrival stamp $\ArrivalTimestamp$ marks the moment the operating system kernel completes the direct memory access (DMA) transfer. It is the software arrival timestamp that @sec-data-hw-vs-sw-timestamps showed corrupting logged velocities; at runtime it corrupts the pose an observation is paired with. Half of the exposure duration, sensor readout, physical transport, and host DMA transfer all elapse before that interrupt fires. Consequently, the arrival offset $\ArrivalStampOffset = \ArrivalTimestamp - {\CaptureTimestamp}_0$ is never zero. Substituting arrival time for capture time directly corrupts downstream state estimation and action generation.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-arrival-stamp
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ARRIVAL-TIMESTAMP OFFSET ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The capture-timestamp paragraph of @sec-perception-handoff.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the error an estimator makes when it dates the navigation
# │          camera's frame at DMA completion instead of at the exposure midpoint.
# │ Show:    26.6 ms from exposure midpoint to DMA completion; 39.9 mm of base
# │          travel at the 1.5 m/s drive limit.
# │ How:     t_recv - t0 = t_exp/2 + t_readout + t_transport + t_dma from
# │          RM.nav_camera and AISLE; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ArrivalStampOffset:
    """Age hidden by an arrival timestamp on the running machine's navigation camera."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time  # category: datasheet
    t_transport = AISLE.t_transport  # category: illustrative
    t_dma = AISLE.t_dma  # category: illustrative
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_recv = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout + t_transport + t_dma).to(millisecond)
    dx_recv = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, tau_recv).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_recv.magnitude - 26.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected arrival offset: {tau_recv}")
    check(abs(dx_recv.magnitude - 39.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected arrival-stamp displacement: {dx_recv}")
    check(tau_recv < AISLE.perception_age, "Arrival offset must be part of the full observation age")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_recv_str = fmt_latency(tau_recv, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    dx_recv_str = fmt_length(dx_recv, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v.to(meter / second), unit=meter / second, precision=1)
```

At constant velocity $\BaseTravelSpeed$, the hidden travel is $\ArrivalOffsetTravel = \BaseTravelSpeed\,\ArrivalStampOffset$. On the mobile manipulator, the navigation camera's frame completes its DMA transfer `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.tau_recv_str` after the exposure midpoint. An estimator that timestamps the frame upon arrival dates the measurement late by that full duration. At the base's `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.v_str` drive limit, this temporal mismatch pairs the visual observation with an estimated pose `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.dx_recv_str` ahead of the physical position the camera occupied at capture.

Eliminating this arrival offset and bounding the camera-to-inertial offset $\CameraImuTimeOffset$ of @sec-perception-transduction-calibration require stamping the capture event directly in hardware rather than recording when a software thread first handles the frame buffer. Software timestamps inherit operating system scheduling jitter, driver queue delays, and thread preemption. While the base rotates at `{python} RollingShutterSkew.omega_yaw_str` rad/s, each millisecond of scheduling jitter misorients the camera by `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dtheta_per_ms_str`, producing a lateral displacement of `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dy_per_ms_jitter_str` at rack-end distance. Two hardware architectures avoid dating capture by software-handler scheduling. In the first architecture, a hardware GPIO strobe (such as FSYNC) from the IMU microcontroller simultaneously latches an inertial sample and triggers the camera exposure. Because this trigger edge marks only the start of exposure for the first sensor row rather than the optical midpoint, the driver must add $\ExposureDuration/2$ to reach the exposure midpoint, plus $\SensorRowIndex\,\RollingShutterRowReadout$ for the specific image row $\SensorRowIndex$ under consideration. Omitting this correction dates the navigation camera frame `{python} CaptureTimingScale.t_trigger_corr_str` early, translating to `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dx_trigger_str` of unmodeled travel at the drive limit. Furthermore, because automatic exposure control varies $\ExposureDuration$ dynamically across frames, the driver must apply the specific exposure time reported in each frame's metadata. In the second architecture, used for networked sensors such as the lidar units and GigE Vision cameras, each peripheral timestamps samples against an onboard hardware clock. The Precision Time Protocol (PTP) [@ieee15882019], or its time-sensitive networking profile gPTP [@ieee8021as2020], disciplines these local clocks to a master reference across the Ethernet bus. @Sec-perception-qualifying-error details how to measure and bound the resulting clock synchronization error.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-extrinsic-error
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EXTRINSIC ANGLE ERRORS AGAINST THE AISLE'S CLEARANCES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The reference-frame paragraph of @sec-perception-handoff, the
# │          transform-chain paragraph of @sec-perception-error-clearance, and
# │          the calibration takeaway.
# │
# │ Goal:    Tie two lever-arm errors to the stopping budget's terms: an
# │          uncalibrated 1 degree mount error at 15 m against the base's side
# │          clearance, and a 0.005 rad extrinsic shift at 10 m against delta_loc.
# │ Show:    0.26 m, about 1.7x the 0.15 m side clearance; 50 mm, the whole
# │          delta_loc allowance.
# │ How:     Delta_y = d sin(theta); delta_x = z theta; AISLE.side_clearance and
# │          AISLE.delta_loc.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_multiple, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ExtrinsicErrorBudget:
    """Lever-arm errors from angular mount errors, set against the aisle clearances."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    theta_frame = 1.0 * degree  # category: illustrative (uncalibrated mount error)
    d_frame = 15.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (detection range)
    theta_ext = 0.005 * radian  # category: illustrative (extrinsic shift after shock)
    z_ext = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (target range)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dy_frame = (d_frame * math.sin(theta_frame.to(radian).magnitude)).to(meter)
    dy_over_side = (dy_frame / side_clearance).to(dimensionless).magnitude
    dx_ext = (z_ext * theta_ext.magnitude).to(millimeter)
    dx_over_loc = (dx_ext / delta_loc).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dy_frame.magnitude - 0.2618) < 0.0005, f"Unexpected 1-degree lever-arm error: {dy_frame}")
    check(dy_frame > side_clearance, "Prose says the 1-degree error exceeds the side clearance")
    check(abs(dx_ext.magnitude - 50.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected extrinsic-shift error: {dx_ext}")
    check(abs(dx_over_loc - 1.0) < 1e-9, "Prose says the extrinsic shift spends all of delta_loc")
    # margin_clearance_slip_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 262 mm, 50 mm and 150 mm.
    check(round(dy_frame.to(millimeter).magnitude) == 262, f"Slip-ladder mount rung drifted: {dy_frame}")
    check(
        abs(delta_loc.to(millimeter).magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9 and abs(side_clearance.to(millimeter).magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-9,
        "Slip-ladder reference lines drifted",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    theta_frame_str = fmt(theta_frame.to(degree).magnitude, precision=0)
    d_frame_str = fmt_length(d_frame, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dy_frame_str = fmt_length(dy_frame, unit=meter, precision=2)
    dy_over_side_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dy_over_side, precision=1)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    theta_ext_str = fmt(theta_ext.magnitude, precision=3)
    z_ext_str = fmt_length(z_ext, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dx_ext_str = fmt_length(dx_ext, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(millimeter), unit=millimeter, precision=0)
```

The second mandatory property is the **reference frame**\index{Reference frame!definition} identifier $\SensorReferenceFrame$. Every spatial measurement is natively resolved in the local coordinate system of the physical transducer: a camera measures bearing angles relative to its optical center, whereas a radar measures range and Doppler velocity relative to its antenna array. Downstream trajectory planners and occupancy maps, by contrast, operate in a chassis body frame $\BodyReferenceFrame$ or an inertial navigation frame $\WorldReferenceFrame$. Transforming an observation from $\SensorReferenceFrame$ to $\BodyReferenceFrame$ requires applying a rigid-body spatial transformation consisting of a rotation matrix and a translation vector that define the sensor mounting extrinsics, the calibrated location and orientation at which the sensor is bolted to the machine. Coordinate frames nest hierarchically from the physical operating environment down to the transducer: $\EarthReferenceFrame \to \MapReferenceFrame \to \OdometryReferenceFrame \to \BodyReferenceFrame \to \SensorReferenceFrame$, where every link in this tree introduces its own transform and uncertainty, as diagrammed in @fig-08-coordinate-frame-tree.

When perception outputs omit the frame identifier or rely on nominal CAD dimensions rather than calibrated physical extrinsics, small angular offsets create large spatial errors that scale with distance. The same uncalibrated yaw error of $\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_frame_str`° that costs `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dy_per_deg_str` at the `{python} CaptureTimingScale.z_str` rack end grows linearly as the planner looks farther down the aisle. For an object at an illustrative range $\TargetRange =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.d_frame_str` down a long aisle, it induces a transverse position error $\ExtrinsicLateralError \approx \TargetRange \sin\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle$ of `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_frame_str`. This lateral offset is approximately `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_over_side_mult_str` the `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.side_clearance_str` side clearance that the base maintains from the warehouse racks, causing the planner to either steer into the racking or falsely reject an open aisle as obstructed.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_clearance_slip_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Five horizontal gray bars in millimeters, longest at top: 1 degree mount error at 15 meters 262 millimeters, dispatch age 77.4, arrival stamp 39.9, row skew 24.9, trigger stamp 12 millimeters. A dotted slate line marks the 50 millimeter localization allowance and a dashed red line marks the 150 millimeter side clearance; only the mount bar crosses the red line."}

*Timing slips cost tens of millimeters; a `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_frame_str`° mount error at `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.d_frame_str` costs `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dy_frame_str`.*
:::

The third mandatory property is an **uncertainty representation**\index{Uncertainty envelope!definition}, such as a measurement covariance $\MeasurementCovariance$ paired with a validated tail bound or hard error envelope when physical clearance depends on it. Environmental degradations such as low illumination, atmospheric scattering, specular reflections, and out-of-distribution neural network errors distort the residual distribution far beyond Gaussian assumptions. While a covariance matrix characterizes second moments, it does not guarantee a conservative bounding volume for the true physical state. Downstream state estimators and policy heads rely on $\MeasurementCovariance$ to weight incoming sensory updates against dynamic motion predictions. If perception reports an artificially optimistic covariance, the estimator over-weights spurious measurements and commands aggressive, erratic actuator responses. Robust physical safety decisions must therefore account explicitly for systematic bias, missed detections, and sensor operational limits alongside the reported covariance.

### Calibrating the coordinate chain {#sec-perception-coordinate-chain}

A coordinate frame transform maps a point expressed relative to one origin into the coordinate system of another. Its rotational component reorients the coordinate axes, while its translational component accounts for the spatial displacement between origins. Homogeneous matrix representations package these operations so that camera-to-wrist, wrist-to-base, and base-to-world relationships can be composed at the exact capture instant ${\CaptureTimestamp}_0$. The engineering requirement is that every link in the kinematic chain describe the true physical mounting and instantaneous pose at that capture time. The notation below writes the destination as a lower index and the source as an upper index, expressing the same mapping direction as the two-subscript convention used for LiDAR de-skewing.

A robot's spatial coordinate system forms a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** of transforms $\TransformGraph = (\TransformGraphVertexSet, \TransformGraphEdgeSet)$, where vertices $\TransformGraphVertexSet = \{\TransformGraphFrame_i\}$ represent physical coordinate frames and directed edges $\TransformGraphEdgeSet$ represent time-varying rigid-body transforms $\Pose_{ij}(\TimeInstant) \in \text{SE}(3)$. In practice, systems constrain this DAG to a directed tree where each non-root frame has exactly one parent, ensuring a unique path between any two frames. When unprojecting an optical observation $\CameraFramePoint({\CaptureTimestamp}_0)$ into world coordinates, the runtime composes the transforms along that tree:
$$\WorldFramePoint({\CaptureTimestamp}_0) = \WorldMapTransform \cdot \MapOdometryTransform({\CaptureTimestamp}_0) \cdot \OdometryBaseTransform({\CaptureTimestamp}_0) \cdot \BaseFlangeTransform({\CaptureTimestamp}_0) \cdot \FlangeCameraTransform \cdot \CameraFramePoint({\CaptureTimestamp}_0)$$
The physical mounting location of the sensor on the kinematic chain dictates how coordinate transforms update across this DAG:

In an **eye-in-hand**\index{Eye-in-hand calibration!definition} configuration, the camera or depth sensor is bolted directly to the manipulator's moving tool flange ($\FlangeReferenceFrame$). Moving any preceding joint alters the sensor's optical center relative to the world, requiring continuous forward kinematics updates. Solving for the rigid extrinsic transform $\EyeInHandUnknownTransform = \FlangeCameraTransform \in \text{SE}(3)$ requires executing robot motions across $\CalibrationRotationAxisCount \ge 2$ non-parallel rotational axes while observing a stationary fiducial target, such as a ChArUco grid.[^fn-charuco-calibration-board] The running machine's wrist camera is mounted this way, which makes this the calibration its grasps depend on. For two distinct poses $\CalibrationPoseIndex$ and $\CalibrationPoseIndex+1$, the closed kinematic loop establishes the classic **hand-eye matrix equation**:[^fn-handeye-calibration-origin]
$$\EyeInHandFlangeMotion \EyeInHandUnknownTransform = \EyeInHandUnknownTransform \EyeInHandCameraMotion$$
where $\EyeInHandFlangeMotion = (\EarlierBaseFlangeTransform)^{-1} \LaterBaseFlangeTransform \in \text{SE}(3)$ is the relative flange displacement reported by the forward kinematics chain, and $\EyeInHandCameraMotion = \EarlierCameraTargetTransform (\LaterCameraTargetTransform)^{-1} \in \text{SE}(3)$ is the relative camera displacement extracted from optical target unprojection.

[^fn-charuco-calibration-board]: **ChArUco Board**: A chessboard whose white squares carry uniquely coded ArUco markers. The chessboard corners give subpixel accuracy and the codes identify which corners are in view, so calibration works from partial views of the board, the usual case for a camera on a moving wrist. \index{Calibration!ChArUco target}

[^fn-handeye-calibration-origin]: **Hand-Eye Calibration**: The problem was posed as $\Glyph{\mathbf{AX}}=\Glyph{\mathbf{XB}}$ independently by @shiu1989calibration and @tsai1989new, for cameras bolted to robot wrists. The camera's pose relative to the flange is never measured directly, only inferred from paired motions, so any error in $\EyeInHandUnknownTransform$ enters every grasp the arm plans from that camera, and poorly spread calibration motions leave it weakly determined. \index{Calibration!hand-eye}

In an **eye-to-hand**\index{Eye-to-hand calibration!definition} calibration rig, the camera overlooks the workspace from a body-mounted mast or a stationary overhead beam. When calibrating against an overhead camera, the mobile base must remain parked so that the camera-to-base transform remains constant ($\EyeToHandUnknownTransform = \BaseCameraTransform \in \text{SE}(3)$), while the target is affixed to the robot's moving end-effector ($\EyeToHandTargetTransform = \FlangeTargetTransform \in \text{SE}(3)$). At each joint configuration, let $\EyeToHandFlangePose = (\BaseFlangeTransform)^{-1}$ map base coordinates into the flange frame and $\EyeToHandCameraPose = (\CameraTargetTransform)^{-1}$ map camera coordinates into the target frame. These are absolute pose transforms for this rig, rather than the relative motions used above. Both paths then map camera coordinates into the flange frame:
$$\EyeToHandFlangePose \EyeToHandUnknownTransform = \EyeToHandTargetTransform \EyeToHandCameraPose$$
If the mobile base subsequently moves relative to the overhead camera, the runtime must update the camera-to-base transform accordingly.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-link-thermal-expansion
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THERMAL EXPANSION OF AN ALUMINUM LINK
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The calibration-drift paragraph of @sec-perception-coordinate-chain.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the length change of a warmed aluminum link.
# │ Show:    23e-6/K x 1 m x 10 K = 0.23 mm.
# │ How:     dL = alpha * L * dT.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, check

class LinkThermalExpansion:
    """Length change of a uniformly warmed aluminum link."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    alpha = 23e-6 / kelvin  # category: illustrative (typical structural aluminum; alloy datasheet supplies the exact value)
    l_link = 1.0 * meter  # category: illustrative (link length)
    d_temp = 10.0 * kelvin  # category: illustrative (uniform warming)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    dl = (alpha * l_link * d_temp).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dl.magnitude - 0.23) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected expansion: {dl}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_str = fmt(alpha.to(1 / kelvin).magnitude * 1e6, precision=0)
    l_link_str = fmt_length(l_link, unit=meter, precision=0)
    d_temp_str = fmt(d_temp.to(kelvin).magnitude, precision=0)
    dl_str = fmt_length(dl, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
```

Treating the nominal rigid transform chain from CAD as an exact physical calibration ignores load and temperature effects. Physical manipulators exhibit mechanical compliance under payload mass, lost motion and torsional wind-up in the joints (strain wave gears have near-zero backlash, but their flexsplines still twist under load), and thermal expansion (structural aluminum expands at $\ThermalExpansionCoefficient \approx$ `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.alpha_str`$\times 10^{-6}/\text{K}$). For an illustrative `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.l_link_str` aluminum link that warms uniformly by `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.d_temp_str`$^\circ\text{C}$, the corresponding expansion is `{python} LinkThermalExpansion.dl_str`. A motor temperature rise alone does not establish that link-temperature change, as localized thermal gradients across structural members and encoder mountings require direct measurement before updating calibration parameters.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-wrist-timestamp-skew
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ JOINT-TO-CAMERA TIMESTAMP SKEW AT THE WRIST
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The joint-kinematics timing paragraph of
# │          @sec-perception-coordinate-chain.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the wrist-camera error from a joint/camera timestamp skew and
# │          the largest skew a grasp tolerance allows.
# │ Show:    10 mm + 3 mm = 13 mm for a 10 ms skew; 3.8 ms allowed for 5 mm.
# │ How:     dp = (v + omega r) dt; dt_max = eps_pos / (v + omega r).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, check

class WristTimestampSkew:
    """Wrist-camera position error from joint/camera timestamp skew."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_wrist = 1.0 * meter / second  # category: illustrative (wrist linear speed)
    omega_wrist = 2.0 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (wrist angular speed)
    r_cam = 0.15 * meter  # category: illustrative (camera lever arm)
    dt_skew = 10.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (unmodeled skew)
    eps_pos = 5.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (grasp position tolerance)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_eff = (v_wrist + omega_wrist.to(1 / second).magnitude * r_cam / second).to(meter / second)
    dp_lin = (v_wrist * dt_skew).to(millimeter)
    dp_rot = ((v_eff - v_wrist) * dt_skew).to(millimeter)
    dp = (dp_lin + dp_rot).to(millimeter)
    dt_max = (eps_pos / v_eff).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(dp.magnitude - 13.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected skew error: {dp}")
    check(abs(dt_max.magnitude - 3.85) < 0.01, f"Unexpected skew bound: {dt_max}")
    check(dt_max > 1.0 * millisecond, "Prose says millisecond-level alignment suffices")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_wrist_str = fmt_velocity(v_wrist, unit=meter / second, precision=0)
    omega_wrist_str = fmt(omega_wrist.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=0)
    r_cam_str = fmt_length(r_cam, unit=meter, precision=2)
    dt_skew_str = fmt_latency(dt_skew, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dp_lin_str = fmt_length(dp_lin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    dp_rot_str = fmt_length(dp_rot, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    dp_str = fmt_length(dp, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    eps_pos_str = fmt_length(eps_pos, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    dt_max_str = fmt_latency(dt_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Fusing joint kinematics with optical frames also requires temporal alignment across the transform DAG. Any uncalibrated timestamp skew $\InterSensorClockSkew = \CameraSampleTimestamp - \JointSampleTimestamp$ between the motor communication bus (such as EtherCAT or CANopen) and the camera exposure window evaluates the forward kinematics chain at stale joint angles $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\JointSampleTimestamp) \neq \GeneralizedCoordinates(\CameraSampleTimestamp)$, inducing spatial tracking error:
$$\WristSkewDisplacement = \WristLinearVelocity \, \InterSensorClockSkew + (\WristAngularVelocity \times \SensorLeverArm) \, \InterSensorClockSkew$$
At an illustrative wrist linear velocity $\BodySpeed =$ `{python} WristTimestampSkew.v_wrist_str` and angular velocity $\AngularSpeed =$ `{python} WristTimestampSkew.omega_wrist_str` rad/s with a camera lever arm $\SensorLeverArmLength =$ `{python} WristTimestampSkew.r_cam_str`, an unmodeled `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dt_skew_str` skew displaces the observation by `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dp_lin_str` plus `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dp_rot_str`, or `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dp_str`. This error causes the arm to miss a grasp whose position tolerance is `{python} WristTimestampSkew.eps_pos_str`. The timing requirement follows directly from that tolerance: the skew must satisfy $\InterSensorClockSkew \le \PositionalTaskTolerance/(\BodySpeed + \AngularSpeed \SensorLeverArmLength)$, which evaluates to `{python} WristTimestampSkew.dt_max_str`. Millisecond-level alignment therefore suffices, whereas microsecond synchronization is unnecessary. Systems typically meet this requirement by timestamping both streams against a single shared clock (a fieldbus distributed clock or a PTP master) and interpolating the high-rate joint stream at the camera's exposure midpoint.

The [REP 105 frame convention](https://reps.openrobotics.org/rep-0105/)\index{Standards!REP 105}[^fn-rep-ros-conventions] names these frames and separates a locally continuous `odom` pose from a globally corrected `map` pose. On the mobile manipulator, $\BodyReferenceFrame$ is the base's `base_link`, tracked through the odometric frame `odom`, and the arm's serial chain maps its mounting flange `tool0` through the joint angles back to `base_link`. @Tbl-08-rep105-tree lists the frame roles and the behavioral rules each consumer follows. A local controller consumes a continuous estimate and rejects unexpected transform jumps, while runtime checks verify transform timestamps and estimator uncertainties before execution.

[^fn-rep-ros-conventions]: **ROS Enhancement Proposal (REP)**: The Robot Operating System records its community conventions as numbered REPs, a process copied from Python's enhancement proposals. REP 105 fixes the meaning of `map`, `odom`, and `base_link` and the continuity each must keep [@meeussen2010rep105], so a frame name written into a record denotes the same physical frame for every consumer that reads it. \index{Standards!ROS Enhancement Proposal}

| Frame         | Parent in this example | Meaning                                     | Consumer rule                                                 |
|:--------------|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `earth`       | root                   | Optional geodetic datum                     | Verify datum before global routing                            |
| `map`         | `earth` if present     | Global localization; corrections may jump   | Keep relocalization jumps out of local feedback               |
| `odom`        | `map`                  | Locally continuous pose estimate; may drift | Track motion locally; monitor uncertainty and discontinuities |
| `base_link`   | `odom`                 | Body-fixed origin                           | Body pose still inherits odometry uncertainty                 |
| `sensor_link` | `base_link`            | Calibrated sensor mounting frame            | Apply time-valid extrinsics and their uncertainty             |

: **REP 105 frame roles for a mobile robot**: A compact example of global, local, body, and sensor frames. REP 105 requires `odom`-relative pose to remain continuous but does not prescribe $\Glyph{C}^1$ smoothness, a covariance growth rate, or fixed accuracy; these require estimator-specific evidence. {#tbl-08-rep105-tree tbl-colwidths="[14,20,32,34]"}

::: {#fig-08-coordinate-frame-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Coordinate frame tree and its consumers**: Each edge states the property REP 105 or calibration gives it and the uncertainty it adds to the prose equation below. Only the odom to base_link edge is required to stay continuous; the map to odom correction may jump at relocalization, so local tracking loops consume the continuous branch while global planners reconcile the jump. A sensor observation reaches the consumers with its frame, capture epoch ${\CaptureTimestamp}_0$, and covariance $\MeasurementCovariance$." fig-alt="Vertical tree of five labeled frame boxes linked by downward arrows: earth, drawn dashed as optional, then map, odom, base_link, and sensor_link. Each arrow carries a short label: fixed datum if present; may jump at relocalization with sigma map; continuous per REP 105 and drifts with sigma odom; rigid and calibrated with sigma ext. Brackets on the right group map as used by the global planner, odom and base_link as used by local tracking loops, and sensor_link as the observation carrying frame, epoch, and covariance."}
![](images/svg/fig08_coordinate_frame_tree.svg){width="90%"}
:::

Splitting consumers across the tree keeps a relocalization jump out of the actuators (@fig-08-coordinate-frame-tree). Global planners absorb the discontinuous $\MapPoseCovariance$ corrections at relocalization, while high-rate local tracking loops consume only the continuous `odom` $\to$ `base_link` branch, so a global correction never reaches the actuators as an abrupt tracking step. Mounting uncertainty still compounds with dynamic pose uncertainty across every intermediate link. Under a first-order propagation model with independent error sources:
$$\WorldPointCovariance = \MapCovarianceJacobian\MapPoseCovariance\MapCovarianceJacobian^\top + \OdometryCovarianceJacobian\OdometryPoseCovariance\OdometryCovarianceJacobian^\top + \ExtrinsicCovarianceJacobian\ExtrinsicCalibrationCovariance\ExtrinsicCovarianceJacobian^\top$$
where the Jacobians $\FunctionJacobian$ project each frame's spatial covariance into world coordinates. When frame errors correlate, the propagation must include their cross-covariance terms. A downstream consumer requires the frame identifier, capture epoch, and compounded uncertainty envelope, rather than a transform selected merely by its latest publication timestamp.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How these sensor-to-body transforms go stale as the joints and base move is developed in @sec-memory-reference-frames.
:::

::: {#psp-perception-observation-invariants .callout-perspective title="The three invariants of observation"}
Pass a perception claim with its capture time and clock domain, coordinate frame, and qualified uncertainty. Refuse a claim when any of those cannot be checked for the proposed motion.
:::

While capture timestamping and kinematic calibration establish the physical instant and spatial reference frame of a measurement, delivering that measurement across an embodied runtime introduces variable computational delay. Managing this latency requires constructing an explicit age budget that tracks the observation from physical energy integration through neural inference and dispatch, bounding the observation's age before downstream actuators act.

## Bounding Observation Age {#sec-perception-age-budget}

Even when a rack-end observation is geometrically calibrated, the data it contains describes the past. Any delivery deadline for perception must therefore account for the full physical interval since photon capture, including the acquisition, transport, and queueing stages that neural inference benchmarks ignore.

::: {#dfn-perception-spatial-information-age .callout-definition title="Observation age"}

***Observation age***\index{Observation age!definition}\index{Spatial information age|see{Observation age}} ($\DispatchObservationAge$), also called spatial information age, is the physical time elapsed between the exposure midpoint at the transducer and the moment perception dispatches the resulting observation. It is the capture-to-dispatch part of the measurement age that @sec-body-measurement-freshness counts from transduction. The observation keeps aging after dispatch, and the age a consumer computes on its own clock when it admits or reuses the observation is its **current evidence age**, which equals $\DispatchObservationAge$ plus the time elapsed since dispatch.

1.  **Significance**: Because the robot continues moving while the compute pipeline runs, observation age converts directly into physical displacement (@eq-percep-spatial-displacement) and expands the stopping budget through the pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, the navigation-camera observation is already `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` old at dispatch, which is `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.dx_str` of blind travel at the `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` drive limit before any downstream consumer has inspected the frame.
2.  **Distinction**: Conventional benchmark latency measures only the software execution time of a forward pass. In contrast, observation age spans the entire physical journey from photon arrival to dispatch: the exposure midpoint, sensor rolling readout, serialized bus transport, direct memory access (DMA) transfers, driver queueing, image signal processor (ISP) conversions, model inference, and inter-process dispatch. Scheduling delay after dispatch belongs to the current evidence age, not to $\DispatchObservationAge$.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Systems engineers frequently confuse a frame's arrival timestamp in userspace memory ($\ArrivalTimestamp$) with its actual physical observation time (${\CaptureTimestamp}_0$). On the navigation camera, the arrival timestamp overlooks `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.tau_recv_str` of front-end exposure, readout, and transport. At the maximum drive limit, this unmeasured interval conceals `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.dx_recv_str` of physical travel, saddling downstream controllers with an unmodeled phase lag.

:::

When evaluated along the machine's trajectory, observation age integrates directly into spatial displacement (@eq-percep-spatial-displacement):
$$\ObservationAgeDisplacement = \int_{{\CaptureTimestamp}_0}^{{\CaptureTimestamp}_0+\DispatchObservationAge} \Velocity(\TimeInstant)\,d\TimeInstant$$ {#eq-percep-spatial-displacement}
Travel is one of three error sources the chapter must bound, and writing them side by side previews where each is bounded. Adding this motion-induced displacement to first-order stereo triangulation noise and small-angle extrinsic error gives a single error scale for the pipeline (@eq-percep-unified-uncertainty-envelope):
$$\PerceptionErrorScale = \underbrace{\int_{{\CaptureTimestamp}_0}^{{\CaptureTimestamp}_0+\DispatchObservationAge} \|\Velocity(\TimeInstant)\|\,d\TimeInstant}_{\text{path-length travel}} + \underbrace{\frac{\TargetRange^2}{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline}\DisparityStandardDeviation}_{\text{stereo depth standard deviation}} + \underbrace{\TargetRange |\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle|}_{\text{small-angle mounting error scale}}$$ {#eq-percep-unified-uncertainty-envelope}
The first term integrates instantaneous speed to compute path length, providing an upper bound on net translation during the perception delay; the latency waterfall below sizes it for the navigation camera. The second term characterizes depth uncertainty for a calibrated stereo camera with baseline $\StereoBaseline$, focal length $\FocalLength$, operating range $\TargetRange$, and disparity standard deviation $\DisparityStandardDeviation$; @sec-perception-error-clearance derives it and evaluates it on an illustrative rig, and it is a standard-deviation scale rather than an absolute bound. The third term models the lever-arm displacement produced by a small extrinsic angular misalignment $\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle$ over target distance $\TargetRange$, the error @sec-perception-handoff already sized at the rack end. The sum is therefore an order-of-magnitude scale, not a safety envelope. It adds magnitudes that point in different directions and leaves out calibration bias and the heavy tail of real residuals, which is why the clearance a consumer holds rests instead on a measured residual quantile (@eq-percep-clearance-inset).

### The latency waterfall {#sec-perception-latency-waterfall}

On the navigation camera, the observation age $\DispatchObservationAge$ defined above accumulates stage by stage, from the exposure midpoint to the moment perception publishes its processed measurement\index{Observation age!latency waterfall}. When hardware stages execute sequentially, the total age expands as a **latency waterfall**\index{Latency waterfall}; if adjacent stages overlap in hardware or stream through pipelined ring buffers, their combined duration replaces the naive sum of individual stage times:
$$\DispatchObservationAge = \frac{\ExposureDuration}{2} + \FrameReadoutTime + \SensorLinkTransportTime + \DmaQueueTime + \IspProcessingTime + \VisionBackboneTime + \PerceptionDispatchTime$$ {#eq-percep-latency-waterfall}

Because a physical robot possesses mechanical momentum, observation age is not an abstract scheduling metric. It translates directly into blind physical displacement:
$$\AgeBlindTravel = \SpeedAtDetection \cdot \DispatchObservationAge$$
While the perception subsystem captures photons, clocks out pixel lines, transfers buffers, and executes network kernels, the chassis keeps moving at velocity $\SpeedAtDetection$. A complete margin must also count the downstream response: expiry of the chunk lease sized in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing, the control tick, fieldbus transmission, and brake onset. Summing these terms yields the partial pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay = \DispatchObservationAge + \ChunkLease + \PermissionLoopPeriod + \CommandTransportTime + \ActuatorResponseTime$, which governs the corresponding subtotal of blind travel:
$$\BlindTravelDistance = \SpeedAtDetection \cdot \PrebrakeDelay$$
At constant operating velocity, every millisecond of unmodeled latency drains physical clearance linearly. Because the permission path runs concurrently on its own MCU, the safety calculation must reflect that dedicated architecture rather than assuming that every stalled neural forward pass postpones emergency braking. Notebook \ref{nbk-perception-sensor-transduction-latency-spatial-information-age} steps through each hardware and software stage of this waterfall for the warehouse mobile manipulator, converting elapsed time into traveled distance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-sensor-information-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAVIGATION-CAMERA INFORMATION AGE AND STOPPING-BUDGET ROW 5
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: \ref{nbk-perception-sensor-transduction-latency-spatial-information-age},
# │          @tbl-08-latency-budget, and the stopping-budget paragraph of
# │          @sec-perception-latency-waterfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Sum the warehouse mobile manipulator's navigation-camera latency
# │          waterfall into t_age and add its term to the stopping budget.
# │ Show:    Stage increments and cumulative ages; t_age 51.6 ms; tau_delay
# │          133.6 ms; row 5 v*t_age 77.4 mm at 1.5 m/s; running total
# │          835.5 mm -> 912.9 mm; 187.1 mm of the 1.10 m clear distance left.
# │ How:     Stage terms from RM.nav_camera and AISLE; totals from
# │          calc_safe_stopping_distance with the Body and Nervous System terms
# │          (a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin, lease path, brake onset). The C2
# │          suffix and tracking inset join later rows, not this one.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class SensorInformationAge:
    """Navigation-camera latency waterfall, t_age, and the observation-age row of the stopping budget."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX477 navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet
    t_transport = AISLE.t_transport.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_dma = AISLE.t_dma.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_isp = AISLE.t_isp.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_backbone = AISLE.t_backbone.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_ipc = AISLE.t_ipc.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_half = (t_exp / 2).to(millisecond)
    t_frame = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    age_after_exposure = t_exp_half
    age_after_readout = age_after_exposure + t_readout
    age_after_transport = age_after_readout + t_transport
    age_after_dma = age_after_transport + t_dma
    age_after_isp = age_after_dma + t_isp
    age_after_backbone = age_after_isp + t_backbone
    tau_age = (age_after_backbone + t_ipc).to(millisecond)

    tau_delay = (tau_age + t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond)
    dx = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, tau_age).to(millimeter)
    row_age = dx
    total_before = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act, a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(millimeter)
    total_after = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v, tau_delay, a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(millimeter)
    remaining = (d_clear - total_after).to(millimeter)
    dx_frame = (v * t_frame).to(millimeter)  # checkpoint: one dropped frame of extra age
    frame_share = (dx_frame / remaining).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_age.magnitude - AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, f"Waterfall disagrees with AISLE.perception_age: {tau_age}")
    check(abs(tau_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected t_age: {tau_age}")
    check(abs(tau_delay.magnitude - AISLE.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, f"Delay sum disagrees with AISLE.tau_delay: {tau_delay}")
    check(abs(tau_delay.magnitude - 133.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected tau_delay: {tau_delay}")
    check(abs(v.magnitude - 1.5) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected drive limit: {v}")
    check(abs(row_age.magnitude - 77.4) < 0.05, f"Unexpected observation-age row: {row_age}")
    check(abs(total_before.magnitude - 835.5) < 0.05, f"Unexpected running total before row 5: {total_before}")
    check(abs(total_after.magnitude - 912.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected running total after row 5: {total_after}")
    check(abs((total_after - total_before - row_age).magnitude) < 1e-6, "Row 5 does not close the running total")
    check(abs(remaining.magnitude - 187.1) < 0.05, f"Unexpected remaining clear distance: {remaining}")
    check(abs(dx_frame.magnitude - 25.0) < 0.05 and 0.13 < frame_share < 0.14, f"Checkpoint answer drifted: {dx_frame}, {frame_share}")
    check(
        t_backbone == max(t_exp_half, t_readout, t_transport, t_dma, t_isp, t_backbone, t_ipc),
        "Notebook says the backbone is the largest single stage",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_exp_half_str = fmt_latency(t_exp_half, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_readout_str = fmt_latency(t_readout, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_transport_str = fmt_latency(t_transport, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_dma_str = fmt_latency(t_dma, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_isp_str = fmt_latency(t_isp, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_backbone_str = fmt_latency(t_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ipc_str = fmt_latency(t_ipc, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_age_str = fmt_latency(tau_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    tau_age_s_str = fmt_time(tau_age.to(second), 'second', precision=4)
    age_after_exposure_str = fmt_latency(age_after_exposure, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    age_after_readout_str = fmt_latency(age_after_readout, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_transport_str = fmt_latency(age_after_transport, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_dma_str = fmt_latency(age_after_dma, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_isp_str = fmt_latency(age_after_isp, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_after_backbone_str = fmt_latency(age_after_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    dx_m_str = fmt_length(dx.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=4)
    dx_mm_str = fmt_length(dx, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    row_age_str = fmt_length(row_age, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    total_before_str = fmt_length(total_before, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    total_after_str = fmt_length(total_after, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    remaining_str = fmt_length(remaining, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=millisecond, precision=1)

    tau_age_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{age}}}} = {t_exp_half_str} + {t_readout_str} + {t_transport_str} + {t_dma_str} + {t_isp_str} + {t_backbone_str} + {t_ipc_str} = {tau_age_str}"
    )
    dx_display_math = fmt_display_math(rf"\Delta x = ({v_str}) \times ({tau_age_s_str}) = {dx_m_str} = {dx_mm_str}")
    t_rest_str = fmt_latency((t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_act).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_delay_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = \underbrace{{t_{{\text{{age}}}}}}_{{{tau_age_str}}} + \underbrace{{T_{{\text{{lease}}}} + T_{{\text{{tick}}}} + T_{{\text{{bus}}}} + T_{{\text{{act}}}}}}_{{{t_rest_str}}} = {tau_delay_str}"
    )
    d_stop_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}}}} = \underbrace{{d_{{\text{{base}}}} + d_{{\text{{lease}}}}}}_{{{total_before_str}}} + \underbrace{{v \cdot t_{{\text{{age}}}}}}_{{{row_age_str}}} = {total_after_str}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-perception-sensor-transduction-latency-spatial-information-age .callout-notebook title="Travel before the frame is read"}

**Problem**: The mobile manipulator drives toward a rack end at its drive limit when a person steps out. How old is the navigation camera's observation of that person when perception dispatches it, and how far has the base traveled by then?

**Variables**:

* Exposure $\ExposureDuration =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_exp_str` (Chosen low-light setting), so the midpoint lag is $\ExposureDuration/2 =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_exp_half_str`; rolling readout $\FrameReadoutTime =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_readout_str` (Datasheet).
* Residual MIPI CSI-2 transport $\SensorLinkTransportTime =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_transport_str` (Illustrative). The [Sony IMX477 flyer](https://www.sony-semicon.com/files/62/pdf/p-13_IMX477-AACK_Flyer.pdf) specifies a four-lane option up to $2.1\text{ Gbps/lane}$; the budget assigns only the transport left after streaming readout, not frame size divided by peak lane rate.
* DMA and driver queue $\DmaQueueTime =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_dma_str`, ISP debayering and rectification $\IspProcessingTime =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_isp_str`, INT8 vision backbone $\VisionBackboneTime =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str`, and covariance packaging with zero-copy dispatch $\PerceptionDispatchTime =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_ipc_str` (all Illustrative).
* Drive limit $\SpeedAtDetection =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` (Illustrative).

**Math**:

*Age at dispatch.* The serial stages of @eq-percep-latency-waterfall sum to
`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_display_math`

*Travel.* Holding speed through the age window:
`{python} SensorInformationAge.dx_display_math`

*Sensitivity.* Each further millisecond in any stage adds `{python} CaptureTimingScale.dx_per_ms_str` of travel at the drive limit.

**Result**: The observation is `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` old at dispatch, and the base has covered `{python} SensorInformationAge.dx_mm_str`. The backbone is the largest single stage, but exposure and readout alone contribute `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_readout_str` before any computation starts.

**Systems insight**: The base covers this distance before the perception record exists. Timestamped pose propagation can place the old observation correctly in the current frame, but no later stage returns the distance already traveled, so $\SpeedAtDetection\,\DispatchObservationAge$ enters the stopping budget as a term of its own.

:::

The seven stages of @tbl-08-latency-budget sum to the observation age at dispatch, $\DispatchObservationAge =$ `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`. Each stage value is a budgeted allocation, the most that stage may take under load, rather than a typical measurement, so the sum is the age the rest of the machine plans against and the last column of the table names the measurement that must confirm it. The stopping budget then adds the active lease and response path of @sec-nervous-lease-sizing:
`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_display_math`
This is the pre-brake delay that @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline and the event timing table of @sec-nervous carried with $\DispatchObservationAge$ entered as a given; its first term is now derived rather than assumed.

This subtotal is a **partial delay budget** rather than an end-to-end capture-to-response bound. In the timing breakdown of @tbl-04-event-timing, perception governs the first interval from capture to dispatch, while actuator mechanics govern the third interval of physical braking. The observation continues to age across the intermediate second interval while the proposer completes inference, transmits the candidate trajectory, and awaits admission from the permission path. Let $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ denote this dispatch-to-admission interval, encompassing model planning and inter-process communication overheads. Because an active lease takes effect only upon candidate admission, the total delay under a stalled-proposer fault equals the displayed subtotal plus $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$. In @sec-placement-dispatch-admission, notebook \ref{nbk-placement-transport-budget} allocates a budget for $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ that awaits empirical validation on hardware. That allocation includes a full inference after dispatch, and part of that inference overlaps the vision backbone already counted in $\DispatchObservationAge$. Adding the two therefore counts the overlap twice and overstates the delay, which errs on the safe side; timestamping both intervals on the loaded machine removes the overlap.

Laid on one clock, the partial budget shows where the unbounded interval sits (@fig-08-capture-to-brake-strip). Everything before dispatch at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str` belongs to perception, everything after it belongs to the response path that reaches brake onset at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_str`, and $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ enters exactly at the dispatch line, so whatever value it takes shifts every later event to the right.

::: {#fig-08-capture-to-brake-strip fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Capture-to-brake timing strip**: Time runs from the exposure midpoint of the frame that first shows the hazard. The camera and host lanes carry the navigation camera's serial stages, with link, DMA, and ISP drawn as one segment, to dispatch at `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`; the response lane adds the lease, tick, bus, and actuator onset of a stalled proposer to reach `{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_delay_str`. The row beneath reads the same axis as base travel at the `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` drive limit. The dashed line at dispatch marks where the dispatch-to-admission interval $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ enters; this chapter does not bound it, so every later event shifts right by its measured value." fig-alt="Horizontal timing strip with three lanes labeled camera, host, and response over a time axis in milliseconds. The camera lane shows a solid exposure bar centered on the capture line and a readout bar after it. The host lane shows a combined link, DMA, and ISP bar, a longer backbone bar, and a thin IPC bar ending at a dispatch line. A dashed line at dispatch is labeled as the point where unbounded dispatch-to-admission time enters. The response lane starts at dispatch with a long lease bar, a thin tick and bus bar, and an onset bar ending at a brake-onset line. A bracket over the strip spans capture to brake onset. A travel row beneath marks millimeters of base travel and the travel before and after dispatch."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-perception-capture-to-brake
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CAPTURE-TO-BRAKE TIMING STRIP (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-08-capture-to-brake-strip in @sec-perception-latency-waterfall.
# │
# │ Goal:    Put the navigation camera's dispatch age and the stalled-proposer
# │          response path on one clock, with the travel each consumes.
# │ Show:    exposure and readout; link, DMA, ISP, backbone, IPC to t_age; the
# │          point where the unbounded Delta_da enters; lease, tick, bus, and
# │          onset to tau_delay; travel at the drive limit.
# │ How:     viz.perception_age_strip (the shared timing-strip family) reads
# │          every duration from AISLE; the guards tie its drawn events to
# │          SensorInformationAge.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim.core.units import millimeter

SIA = SensorInformationAge

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v_strip = SIA.v  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
strip_08 = viz.perception_age_strip(AISLE, v_strip)
t_dispatch_drawn = next(e.t for e in strip_08.events if e.label.startswith("dispatch"))
t_onset_drawn = next(e.t for e in strip_08.events if e.label == "brake onset")

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(t_dispatch_drawn - SIA.tau_age.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The strip's dispatch must equal t_age.")
check(abs(t_onset_drawn - SIA.tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "The strip's brake onset must equal tau_delay.")
check(
    abs(strip_08.speed_mm_per_unit * t_dispatch_drawn - SIA.row_age.to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-6,
    "The travel to dispatch must equal the observation-age row.",
)

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for _s in strip_08.spans:  # at print width the 20 ms onset box takes its label on two lines
    if _s.label.startswith("onset "):
        _s.label = _s.label.replace("onset ", "onset\n")
strip_08.figsize = (6.4, 5.4)  # print scale: the strip's default canvas is 10 in wide
fig, ax, axd = viz.plot_timing_strip(strip_08)
plt.show()
```

:::

Because the permission path validates geometric safety without reprocessing raw images, it cannot retroactively compress this perception pipeline delay; the age reaches it strictly through the proposal's stamped evidence epoch. At the `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` drive limit, the observation-age term $\SpeedAtDetection\,\DispatchObservationAge$ contributes `{python} SensorInformationAge.row_age_str` of blind displacement. That travel is the fifth row of the stopping budget. The first three rows are the Body's terms from @eq-body-stopping-distance, braking distance $\SpeedAtDetection^2/2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$, the overhead $\LocalizationBound + \ProtectiveClearanceMargin$, and brake-onset travel $\SpeedAtDetection\,\ActuatorResponseTime$, written together below as $\BaseStoppingDistance$. The fourth row is the lease-path travel $\LeasePathTravel = \SpeedAtDetection\,(\ChunkLease + \PermissionLoopPeriod + \CommandTransportTime)$ of @sec-nervous-lease-sizing. Adding the fifth row gives
`{python} SensorInformationAge.d_stop_display_math`
This additional term raises the partial stopping distance from `{python} SensorInformationAge.total_before_str` to `{python} SensorInformationAge.total_after_str`. Although `{python} SensorInformationAge.remaining_str` remains within the nominal `{python} SensorInformationAge.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance, that remainder cannot be claimed as safety buffer. It must still absorb the travel during the dispatch-to-admission interval $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$, the extra distance of a jerk-limited rather than instantaneous brake application (@sec-planning-base-stopping-budget), and the tracking inset of @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes. This analysis sizes the perception subsystem's contribution to the stopping budget and clarifies the empirical measurements required before an integrated motion claim can be certified; the final column of @tbl-08-latency-budget names that measurement stage by stage.

| Stage              |                                       Increment |                                  Serial age after stage | What to verify                          |
|:-------------------|------------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------------------:|:----------------------------------------|
| Exposure midpoint  |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_exp_half_str` |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_exposure_str` | Exposure and row timestamp convention   |
| Rolling readout    |   `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_readout_str` |   `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_readout_str` | Selected row and overlap with streaming |
| Residual transport | `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_transport_str` | `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_transport_str` | Selected sensor mode and host receiver  |
| DMA and queue      |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_dma_str` |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_dma_str` | Arbitration and queue tail              |
| ISP                |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_isp_str` |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_isp_str` | Mode and competing jobs                 |
| Vision backbone    |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_backbone_str` |  `{python} SensorInformationAge.age_after_backbone_str` | Workload, clock, thermal state          |
| Dispatch           |       `{python} SensorInformationAge.t_ipc_str` |         **`{python} SensorInformationAge.tau_age_str`** | Capture-to-dispatch age and queue tail  |

: **Serial observation-age budget**: The navigation camera's budgeted stage increments, assumed nonoverlapping, sum to its observation age at dispatch. A real pipeline can overlap readout, transfer, and processing, so capture-to-dispatch age requires an end-to-end measurement including queueing tails. Later consumers must add their elapsed post-dispatch interval. {#tbl-08-latency-budget tbl-colwidths="[24,18,20,38]"}

::: {#chk-percep-spatial-info-age .callout-checkpoint title="Observation age and the stopping budget"}

Observation age is paid in travel before any consumer can react, and no later stage returns it.

- [ ] **Observation age**: Can you explain how the interval from the exposure midpoint to dispatch converts into travel that erodes the stopping clearance before a policy can react?
- [ ] **Exposure midpoint vs. arrival timestamp**: Can you explain why dating a frame at DMA completion rather than at its exposure midpoint pairs the observation with the wrong pose?
- [ ] **Pose propagation from capture time**: Can you explain how propagating the machine's pose forward from an observation's capture time places an old observation correctly in the current frame, and why that propagation cannot return the distance already traveled?
- [ ] **Observation age in the stopping budget**: Can you explain why the observation-age term $\SpeedAtDetection\,\DispatchObservationAge$ adds to the stopping distance, and why the permission path, which never reads the image, cannot shorten it?
- [ ] **Dropped-frame estimate**: If a dropped frame leaves a proposal resting on the previous frame, one frame period (`{python} SensorInformationAge.t_frame_str`) older, how much travel does that add at the `{python} SensorInformationAge.v_str` drive limit, and what share of the `{python} SensorInformationAge.remaining_str` remainder does it consume?

:::

### Dating the machine's LiDAR {#sec-perception-lidar-age}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-lidar-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LIDAR AGE AT THE RACK END: STREAMED SECTOR VS FULL SWEEP
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-perception-lidar-age and @tbl-08-lidar-age.
# │
# │ Goal:    Compare two acquisition/processing allocations with the camera
# │          allocation; actual evidence ages require one consumer clock.
# │ Show:    the aisle ahead subtends 61.2 degrees, swept in 8.5 ms; age before
# │          processing 19.5 ms streamed vs 61.0 ms full sweep (with 10 ms data
# │          latency and a 1 ms PTP bound); 32.1 ms left for de-skew and
# │          occupancy extraction within the camera's 51.6 ms allocation;
# │          scan/frame phase, reuse, and downstream waiting remain separate.
# │ How:     RM.lidar.scan_rate; AISLE.aisle_width and AISLE.d_clear; Ouster OS1
# │          Rev7 datasheet data latency (< 10 ms) and PTP accuracy (< 1 ms)
# │          from the registry; AISLE.perception_age.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LidarAge:
    """Age of the OS1-64's rack-end sector under two consumption policies."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_sweep = (1 / RM.lidar.scan_rate).to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet (20 Hz mode)
    aisle_width = AISLE.aisle_width  # category: illustrative
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    t_data = RM.lidar.nominal_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 data latency upper bound)
    eps_ptp = RM.lidar.time_sync_accuracy.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 PTP accuracy upper bound)
    t_camera = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    half_width = (aisle_width / 2).to(meter)
    sector_deg = 2 * math.degrees(math.atan((half_width / d_clear).to(dimensionless).magnitude))
    t_sector = (t_sweep * sector_deg / 360.0).to(millisecond)
    age_stream = (t_sector + t_data + eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    age_full = (t_sweep + t_data + eps_ptp).to(millisecond)
    dx_stream = (v * age_stream).to(millimeter)
    dx_full = (v * age_full).to(millimeter)
    slack_stream = (t_camera - age_stream).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(sector_deg - 61.2) < 0.05, f"Unexpected forward sector: {sector_deg}")
    check(abs(t_sector.magnitude - 8.5) < 0.05, f"Unexpected sector time: {t_sector}")
    check(abs(age_stream.magnitude - 19.5) < 0.05, f"Unexpected streamed age: {age_stream}")
    check(abs(age_full.magnitude - 61.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected full-sweep age: {age_full}")
    check(age_full > t_camera, "The full-sweep preprocessing allocation exceeds the camera allocation")
    check(abs(slack_stream.magnitude - 32.1) < 0.05, f"Unexpected streamed slack: {slack_stream}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_sweep_str = fmt_latency(t_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    aisle_width_str = fmt_length(aisle_width.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    sector_deg_str = fmt(sector_deg, precision=1)
    t_sector_str = fmt_latency(t_sector, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_data_str = fmt_latency(t_data, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    eps_ptp_str = fmt_latency(eps_ptp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    age_stream_str = fmt_latency(age_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_full_str = fmt_latency(age_full, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    dx_stream_str = fmt_length(dx_stream, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    dx_full_str = fmt_length(dx_full, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_camera_str = fmt_latency(t_camera, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    slack_stream_str = fmt_latency(slack_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

The permission path's clearance check inspects range returns from the mobile base's Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR, whose timing structure differs fundamentally from that of the optical camera. A rolling-shutter camera exposes and reads out a discrete frame grid. In contrast, a spinning mechanical LiDAR continuously fires laser diodes and timestamps each azimuth column at the firing instant, disciplined by the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP). Because every point carries an individual capture epoch, the scan lacks a singular frame time. The age of the resulting rack-end spatial estimate is therefore governed by how long the software pipeline buffers returns before releasing the angular sector facing the hazard.

At the configured scan rate, one mechanical revolution requires `{python} LidarAge.t_sweep_str`. At a clear distance of `{python} LidarAge.d_clear_str`, the `{python} LidarAge.aisle_width_str` aisle subtends a forward azimuth sector of `{python} LidarAge.sector_deg_str`°, which the sensor sweeps in `{python} LidarAge.t_sector_str`. @Tbl-08-lidar-age compares two ingestion architectures for handling this point stream: streaming sector packets to consumers immediately upon arrival vs. buffering the entire sweep before dispatching a complete 360° point cloud.

| Stage                                    |              Stream the forward sector |              Wait for the full sweep | Source                             |
|:-----------------------------------------|---------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------|
| Acquisition of the oldest relevant point |       `{python} LidarAge.t_sector_str` |      `{python} LidarAge.t_sweep_str` | Scan rate and aisle geometry       |
| Sensor data latency, upper bound         |         `{python} LidarAge.t_data_str` |       `{python} LidarAge.t_data_str` | Datasheet                          |
| Clock-conversion bound (PTP)             |        `{python} LidarAge.eps_ptp_str` |      `{python} LidarAge.eps_ptp_str` | Datasheet; measure on the machine  |
| Upper age before processing              | **`{python} LidarAge.age_stream_str`** | **`{python} LidarAge.age_full_str`** | Computed                           |
| Travel at the drive limit                |      `{python} LidarAge.dx_stream_str` |      `{python} LidarAge.dx_full_str` | Computed                           |
| De-skew and occupancy extraction         |                   Needs measured value |                 Needs measured value | Host measurement under camera load |

: **LiDAR age at the rack end**: The OS1-64's upper age before host processing under two consumption policies, at the configured scan rate. Data latency and clock accuracy are the datasheet's upper bounds; processing time must be measured on the machine under the synchronized camera and inference load. {#tbl-08-lidar-age tbl-colwidths="[30,22,22,26]"}

Waiting for a full revolution consumes `{python} LidarAge.age_full_str` before host computation begins, exceeding the camera's `{python} LidarAge.t_camera_str` acquisition/processing allocation. In contrast, streaming the forward azimuth sector immediately leaves `{python} LidarAge.slack_stream_str` of processing headroom within that allocation for motion de-skew and occupancy extraction. This arithmetic compares pipeline allocations; different scan and frame phases, buffered reuse, and downstream waiting still determine which selected observation is older at consumption. The real-time latency budget dictates the architectural choice: the robot streams and processes sector packets incrementally, propagating individual point timestamps rather than a single aggregated sweep time.

Two strands of evidence therefore meet at the rack end, and the oldest required capture sets the shared age charge. The proposal is anchored to the camera's frame epoch, while the admission check rests on LiDAR range. The permission path must date both on its own clock at the same admission or tick, including bounded clock uncertainty. Streaming fits the illustrated camera-sized acquisition/processing allocation only when de-skew, occupancy extraction, and any phase, reuse, or waiting allowance required by the selected consumption policy fit the `{python} LidarAge.slack_stream_str` headroom. Sharing the camera's row-five charge further requires that the actual LiDAR capture be no older than the camera capture supporting the proposal at that common check. Otherwise the budget must charge the older required evidence, with each elapsed interval counted once. The dispatch-to-admission interval remains a separate downstream charge. Neither strand includes the internal latency of the certified safety scanner, because its worst-case response time is a factory-certified parameter accounted for separately in the scanner's own timing budget described in @sec-enforcement-composite-budget.

Per-column timestamps also enable continuous motion de-skew. Over a single LiDAR revolution at full speed, the mobile base translates `{python} LidarSweep.dx_sweep_str`; the state estimator eliminates this distortion by interpolating robot odometry at each return's precise firing timestamp (@sec-perception-transduction-calibration).

While the optical camera avoids rotational sweeping delays, its serial latency budget has no spare stage to absorb arbitrary queueing, because row five charges exactly the budgeted age. In particular, collecting consecutive frames into multi-frame batches introduces substantial latency penalties before host memory contention is even considered.

### Temporal batching

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-temporal-batching
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TEMPORAL BATCHING ON THE NAVIGATION CAMERA
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The temporal-batching paragraph of @sec-perception-age-budget.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show what a four-frame batch collected across capture times adds
# │          to the navigation camera's observation age.
# │ Show:    16.7 ms frame period at 60 Hz; waits of 50.0, 33.3, and 16.7 ms;
# │          age 51.6 ms -> 101.6 ms, roughly double.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera.frame_rate; AISLE.perception_age; the oldest of
# │          n frames waits (n - 1) frame periods.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class TemporalBatching:
    """Age added by batching successive navigation-camera frames."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_frame = RM.nav_camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    n_batch = 4  # category: illustrative (batch size)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    wait_1 = ((n_batch - 1) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    wait_2 = ((n_batch - 2) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    wait_3 = ((n_batch - 3) * t_period).to(millisecond)
    t_age_batched = (t_age + wait_1).to(millisecond)
    ratio = (t_age_batched / t_age).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_frame.to(hertz).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected frame rate: {f_frame}")
    check(abs(wait_1.magnitude - 50.0) < 0.05, f"Unexpected oldest-frame wait: {wait_1}")
    check(abs(t_age_batched.magnitude - 101.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected batched age: {t_age_batched}")
    check(1.8 < ratio < 2.2, f"Prose says batching roughly doubles the age: {ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    wait_1_str = fmt_latency(wait_1, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    wait_2_str = fmt_latency(wait_2, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    wait_3_str = fmt_latency(wait_3, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_batched_str = fmt_latency(t_age_batched, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Batching amortizes kernel launch overhead and maximizes systolic-array utilization on modern accelerators, but accumulating frames across successive capture times ages the earliest samples. At the navigation camera's `{python} TemporalBatching.f_frame_str` sampling rate ($\CameraFramePeriod \approx$ `{python} TemporalBatching.t_period_str`), forming a batch of four consecutive frames requires holding the first frame for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_1_str`, the second for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_2_str`, and the third for `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_3_str`, while only the fourth enters immediately. Appending this `{python} TemporalBatching.wait_1_str` queueing delay to the baseline `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.t_age_str` observation age roughly doubles total age to `{python} TemporalBatching.t_age_batched_str`. Because row five of the stopping budget charges only the single-frame age, the observation contract at the end of this chapter sets its dispatch threshold at that age plus a sub-millisecond clock bound (@sec-perception-observation-contract), so the batched frame is refused before candidate admission begins. When multi-camera systems synchronize exposure pulses in hardware, grouping frames from distinct sensors across spatial dimensions can improve throughput safely; however, temporal batching across successive timestamps directly erodes closed-loop timeliness.

### Observation age and feedback stability

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-phase-margin-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PHASE MARGIN SPENT BY OBSERVATION AGE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The phase-margin paragraph of @sec-perception-age-budget
# │          and its margin figure.
# │
# │ Goal:    Turn a nominal phase margin at crossover into the delay ceiling
```
