```{python}
# │          a pure age may spend, and show how much of it a 60 ms age uses.
# │ Show:    45 deg at 10 rad/s -> 78.5 ms ceiling; 60 ms uses 76.4 percent.
# │ How:     A pure delay tau removes phase omega_c * tau, so the ceiling is
# │          PM_nom / omega_c (@sec-appendix-control-zoh).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

class PhaseMarginAge:
    """Delay ceiling set by a nominal phase margin at crossover."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    omega_c = 10.0  # category: illustrative (gain crossover, rad/s)
    pm_nom_deg = 45.0  # category: illustrative (nominal phase margin, degrees)
    t_used = 60.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (exposure, transport, and inference)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    pm_nom_rad = math.radians(pm_nom_deg)
    f_c = omega_c / (2 * math.pi)
    tau_max = (pm_nom_rad / omega_c * second).to(millisecond)
    frac_used = (t_used / tau_max).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_max.magnitude - 78.54) < 0.01, f"Unexpected delay ceiling: {tau_max}")
    check(0.76 < frac_used < 0.77, f"Unexpected share of margin used: {frac_used}")
    check(t_used < tau_max, "The example age must sit below the ceiling")
    # margin_phase_margin_erosion_knee.svg fig-alt hand-types PM 45 degrees, 60 ms and 78.5 ms.
    check(pm_nom_deg == 45.0 and abs(t_used.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Phase-margin margin labels drifted")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    omega_c_str = fmt(omega_c, precision=0)
    f_c_str = fmt(f_c, precision=1)
    pm_nom_deg_str = fmt(pm_nom_deg, precision=0)
    pm_nom_rad_str = fmt(pm_nom_rad, precision=3)
    tau_max_str = fmt_latency(tau_max, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_used_str = fmt_latency(t_used, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    frac_used_pct_str = fmt_percent(frac_used, precision=1, style="prose")
```

Beyond draining physical stopping distance, observation age also spends the phase margin of any feedback loop closed through perception, the extra lag that loop can absorb before its corrections reinforce the motion they were meant to damp. @Sec-nervous-time-constants-phase-lag establishes that a pure delay removes phase in proportion to frequency without changing loop gain, so a loop with nominal phase margin $\text{PM}_{\text{nom}}$ at gain crossover frequency $\CrossoverFrequency$\index{Control!gain crossover} has no margin left once $\DispatchObservationAge \ge \text{PM}_{\text{nom}}/\CrossoverFrequency$. Perception draws on that same account. A visual-servoing tracking loop crosses over at `{python} PhaseMarginAge.omega_c_str` rad/s (approximately `{python} PhaseMarginAge.f_c_str` Hz) with a nominal phase margin of `{python} PhaseMarginAge.pm_nom_deg_str`$^\circ$ (`{python} PhaseMarginAge.pm_nom_rad_str` rad). With no other delay charged, its nominal zero-margin ceiling for this perception contribution is $\MaximumObservationAge = \text{PM}_{\text{nom}}/\CrossoverFrequency =$ `{python} PhaseMarginAge.tau_max_str`. If sensor exposure, transport, and neural inference consume `{python} PhaseMarginAge.t_used_str`, the perception pipeline spends `{python} PhaseMarginAge.frac_used_pct_str` of the loop's stability allowance before motor commands are even computed. Whether the integrated loop remains adequately damped requires qualification of its complete dynamics and delays.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_phase_margin_erosion_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Line labeled PM 45 degrees falling linearly with age, with a dot marked 60 milliseconds, crossing a dashed zero line at a red dot marked 78.5 milliseconds; beyond it the line turns red in a light red region labeled unstable, where the nominal phase reserve is exhausted."}

*Delay spends phase margin linearly; at `{python} PhaseMarginAge.tau_max_str` none remains.*
:::

The perception contribution to both checks spends the same elapsed duration in different currencies. Phase lag erodes closed-loop stability, while displacement consumes forward clearance ($\AgeBlindTravel = \SpeedAtDetection \cdot \DispatchObservationAge$), so each consequence is checked on its own terms and the latency is never counted twice in the stopping budget. Rigorous capture timestamps, qualified reference frames, and explicit error bounds make these physical consequences observable throughout the software stack. Even when zero-copy DMA architectures eliminate intermediate buffer copies during host ingestion, memory controller arbitration and bus contention continue to introduce subtle waiting times.

## Ingestion Overhead and Memory Bus Contention {#sec-perception-cost-ingestion}

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-naive-ingestion-copies
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAIVE MULTI-CAMERA INGESTION COPY TRAFFIC
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The naive-baseline paragraph of @sec-perception-cost-ingestion.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the copy traffic when four 1080p60 RGB streams are copied
# │          three times on their way to the accelerator.
# │ Show:    4 x 1920 x 1080 x 3 B x 60 Hz = 1.5 GB/s per copy; 4.5 GB/s total.
# │ How:     rate = cameras x pixels x bytes/pixel x frame rate x copies.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_frequency, check

class NaiveIngestionCopies:
    """Copy traffic of a naive user-space multi-camera ingestion path."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_cam = 4  # category: illustrative (camera count)
    px = 1920 * 1080  # category: definitional (1080p frame)
    bytes_px = 3  # category: illustrative (24-bit RGB after conversion)
    f_cam = 60.0 * hertz  # category: illustrative (frame rate)
    n_copies = 3  # category: illustrative (driver ring, user space, device memory)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    per_copy = (n_cam * px * bytes_px * byte * f_cam).to(gigabyte / second)
    total = (per_copy * n_copies).to(gigabyte / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(per_copy.magnitude - 1.493) < 0.01, f"Unexpected per-copy rate: {per_copy}")
    check(total > 4.0 * gigabyte / second, f"Unexpected total copy rate: {total}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    f_cam_str = fmt_frequency(f_cam, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    per_copy_str = fmt_bandwidth(per_copy, unit=gigabyte / second, precision=1)
    total_str = fmt_bandwidth(total, unit=gigabyte / second, precision=1)
```

A common architectural pitfall in early physical AI prototypes is connecting multiple high-resolution cameras through standard USB or Ethernet ports and ingesting frames using naive user-space libraries, such as OpenCV's `VideoCapture` or default ROS image transport nodes. In this unoptimized baseline, every incoming frame is copied from kernel USB request blocks into a driver ring buffer, copied a second time into user-space process memory, and copied a third time across the PCIe bus into GPU memory. For four 1080p cameras streaming 24-bit color at `{python} NaiveIngestionCopies.f_cam_str`, each copy stage moves `{python} NaiveIngestionCopies.per_copy_str`, meaning the pipeline churns through about `{python} NaiveIngestionCopies.total_str` of continuous memory copies. This overhead generates substantial memory traffic and CPU copying work, though the exact utilization depends on host core capabilities, memory architecture, and pixel format. That data rate alone does not establish CPU saturation or accelerator starvation, but it wastes memory bus bandwidth and cache capacity that concurrent real-time inference urgently requires.

Real-time physical systems avoid this collapse by treating pixel ingestion as a zero-copy DMA\index{Memory!DMA} hardware pipeline. Raw pixel streams arriving over dedicated camera buses bypass CPU copying entirely, writing frames directly into shared physical DRAM before any software thread touches the data. On a shared application processor, however, these camera writes still contend for memory service before inference can read them, and unmanaged bursts can delay host reads or overrun a receiver FIFO and drop a frame.

### MIPI CSI-2 DMA ingress and zero-copy buffers

Once analog-to-digital converters on the sensor die digitize the accumulated pixel charges, the frame travels across a physical interconnect to host memory. Camera streams enter the application processor over the MIPI CSI-2\index{MIPI CSI-2!host ingress} bus.[^fn-mipi-csi2-interface]

[^fn-mipi-csi2-interface]: **MIPI CSI-2 (Mobile Industry Processor Interface, Camera Serial Interface 2)**\index{Hardware!MIPI CSI-2}: The MIPI Alliance's point-to-point camera link streams serialized pixels from the sensor straight to an application processor's receiver and DMA controller, over differential D-PHY lanes or three-wire C-PHY trios, with no network stack between them. That directness is why the camera's transport term in @tbl-08-latency-budget is set by sensor mode and lane rate rather than by protocol processing.

::: {#psp-perception-silicon-ingestion-dataflow-architecture .callout-perspective title="Silicon ingestion dataflow architecture"}
1. **D-PHY / C-PHY physical layer**: Physical lanes serialize pixel packets at the selected sensor and receiver's supported rate; packet headers carry error checks.
2. **System-on-chip (SoC) CSI-2 host controller**: Deserializes byte packets, strips headers, and validates CRC integrity.
3. **Scatter-gather DMA controller**: A dedicated DMA engine transfers pixel byte words directly into DRAM over the internal system interconnect (for example, an AXI crossbar).
4. **Kernel DMA ring buffers**: A Linux `v4l2` driver can map capture buffers into user space.
:::

Once DMA write completion occurs, the kernel capture driver (V4L2, the Linux video-capture interface) issues an interrupt. To eliminate user-space copies, modern embedded Linux systems export DMA buffers directly through the Linux `dma_buf` subsystem. Rather than following the naive three-copy path (Kernel DMA buffer $\to$ User-space buffer $\to$ Pinned host memory $\to$ GPU VRAM), `dma_buf` allows the hardware Image Signal Processor (ISP), CPU, and GPU to import and share identical physical DRAM pages through system IOMMU[^fn-iommu-dmabuf-sharing] page tables. A zero-copy buffer handoff eliminates bulk CPU copying, but DMA arbitration, synchronization, queueing, and consumer scheduling still contribute to ingestion latency. Format conversion, layout changes, or device alignment constraints can still require a targeted transform, but the bulk pixel payload never traverses the CPU cache hierarchy. On a platform without hardware I/O cache coherency, the buffer handoff must explicitly synchronize ownership for the intended consumer. CPU access requires the platform's DMA-to-CPU cache maintenance primitives; accelerator access requires corresponding device mapping, completion ordering, and device-side cache invalidation. Flushing or invalidating the CPU cache alone does not guarantee that an independent neural accelerator will read current pixel values. These synchronization and cache maintenance operations belong directly in the measured ingestion budget.

[^fn-iommu-dmabuf-sharing]: **IOMMU (Input-Output Memory Management Unit)**: The device-side counterpart of the CPU's MMU. It translates the addresses a DMA engine issues through page tables the kernel controls, so the ISP, CPU, and GPU can share one set of physical pages without copying while each device stays confined to its own mappings. A translation miss on that path is one more source of ingestion delay that the measured budget must include. \index{Memory!IOMMU}

Interface selection balances cable reach and mechanical routing flexibility against transport, queueing, and copying overhead. MIPI CSI-2 supports direct sensor ingress to the SoC; serializer/deserializer links extend that path across the machine over multi-meter automotive wiring; USB introduces a host protocol stack and driver buffering whose timing penalty must be measured empirically. The stage breakdown in @tbl-08-latency-budget locates those costs for the selected MIPI path. Any alternative interface requires its own measured stage budget, because an interface specification alone does not determine end-to-end latency. Sensor operating modes, inference workloads, and host memory contention must all mirror the intended deployment conditions.

### Memory bus contention and observation age

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-host-contention-allowance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HOST CONTENTION THE RENEWAL-JITTER ALLOWANCE TOLERATES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The memory-bus contention paragraph of @sec-perception-cost-ingestion.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size how much application-processor contention the chunk stream
# │          can absorb before a healthy proposer's renewals leave the lease
# │          rule's jitter allowance, and when a late renewal lapses the lease.
# │ Show:    50 ms chunk period; 5 ms renewal-jitter allowance; a 12.5 percent
# │          ratio to 40 ms inference (conditional one-for-one admission delay);
# │          the lease lapses at 10 ms late.
# │ How:     Chunk period from RM.chunk_rate; inference from
# │          RM.chunk_inference_latency; lease from AISLE.t_lease; the 5 ms
# │          allowance is the lease rule's chosen value (@sec-nervous-lease-sizing).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class HostContentionAllowance:
    """Application-processor contention absorbed by the lease's renewal-jitter allowance."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen
    t_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance of the lease rule, @sec-nervous-lease-sizing)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period = (1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond)
    t_lapse = (t_lease - t_period).to(millisecond)
    stretch = (t_jitter / t_infer).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk period: {t_period}")
    check(abs(t_jitter.to(millisecond).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected renewal-jitter allowance: {t_jitter}")
    check(t_period + t_jitter < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")
    check(abs(t_lapse.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected lapse point: {t_lapse}")
    check(abs(t_lease.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Margin figure draws a 60 ms lease: {t_lease}")
    check(t_infer < t_period, "Chunk inference must fit inside one chunk period")
    check(abs(stretch - 0.125) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected inference stretch: {stretch}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_jitter.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lapse_str = fmt_latency(t_lapse, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    stretch_pct_str = fmt_percent(stretch, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The raw bandwidth requirements of the mobile manipulator's navigation and wrist cameras are sized in notebook \ref{nbk-data-ingestion-bandwidth-storage-budgets-multi-camera} of @sec-data-telemetry-ingestion-storage. When the perception stack reads those frames, transforms intermediate buffers, and the accelerator fetches model weights and writes activations, the memory controller carries several times that ingress rate. Even that aggregate volume sits comfortably within the memory subsystem's peak bandwidth when averaged over a one-second window.

Average bandwidth does not determine the latency of individual read transactions. On edge robotics SoCs such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the CPU cluster, deep learning accelerator (DLA), GPU, and CSI-2 DMA engines share a single physical DRAM bus in a Unified Memory Architecture (UMA). Synchronized cameras concentrate their DMA writes into sharp microbursts, saturating memory channels and triggering widespread DRAM bank conflicts. When multiple cameras dump uncached raster lines across the system crossbar simultaneously, they repeatedly open and close DRAM page buffers across active banks. If the neural accelerator attempts to stream transformer model weights and intermediate activation tensors during this exact window, memory controller arbitration stalls accelerator read requests behind high-priority sensor DMA streams. These memory read stalls introduce pipeline bubbles into hardware tensor cores, stretching neural inference latency and inflating its tail ($\text{p99}$ jitter). The magnitude of this latency stretch depends on the platform, its interconnect arbitration policy, and the concurrent camera load. Rather than assuming nominal inference latency, engineers must measure tail stretch directly on physical hardware under the synchronized camera workload; the safety lease below constrains the loaded end-to-end renewal interval.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Contention for the shared memory system, and how it would stall the permission tick on a shared-die placement, are developed in @sec-placement-resource-contention.
:::

On the mobile manipulator, this burst lands only on the application processor. Because the permission path executes on its own microcontroller and reads its state from isolated SRAM, a memory burst cannot stretch its safety tick\index{Bus jitter}; rejecting a shared-die placement removed that hazard. Contention on the application processor reaches the permission path only through two observable timing channels: the age of the frame used to construct an action proposal, and the lateness of the renewal message sent by the chunk policy. These two paths have fundamentally different timing allowances. A frame that waits behind camera and accelerator traffic reaches dispatch older than the budgeted stages. The observation contract of @sec-perception-observation-contract sets the dispatch threshold at exactly the budgeted age, because a frame any older would spend travel that row five does not charge, so the permission path refuses every proposal built on that delayed frame.

A chunk policy whose inference stalls behind that same memory traffic renews the execution lease late. Under the coupled budget rule of @sec-nervous-coupled-budget, the lease reserves `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_jitter_str` of renewal jitter above the `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_period_str` chunk period. The ratio to the chunk policy's `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_infer_str` inference is `{python} HostContentionAllowance.stretch_pct_str`, a conditional sensitivity when incremental inference delay reaches admission one-for-one. The actual allowance constrains inter-admission jitter, so the inference stretch it tolerates depends on the renewal schedule and the scheduling, transmission, validation, and mailbox delays sharing that allowance. Qualification must measure the loaded end-to-end inter-admission interval. A renewal that arrives `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_lapse_str` late causes the lease to lapse, triggering a deterministic stop. When physical isolation, frame-age validation, and feasible fallback maneuvers remain intact, excess contention compromises availability rather than safety: the permission path strictly refuses any action delayed beyond the qualified budget. That guarantee holds only so long as those architectural premises and uncorrupted local sensor evidence remain intact.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_renewal_jitter_lease_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Time strip from 45 to 62 milliseconds: a slate tick marks the renewal due at 50, a slate band marks the 5 millisecond allowed lateness to 55, and a dashed red line marks the lease lapse at 60 with a light red wash beyond it; a dimension arrow from 50 to 60 is labeled 10 milliseconds late."}
*A renewal may run `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_jitter_str` late; at `{python} HostContentionAllowance.t_lapse_str` late the lease lapses.*
:::

The duration of a bus-saturating burst also threatens the camera interface itself. Ingest engines rely on direct memory access ring buffers with double or triple buffering to decouple hardware arrival interrupts from consumer reading threads. If host memory bus contention delays DMA completion beyond what the CSI-2 receiver hardware FIFO can buffer, the receiver suffers an overrun and silently drops the frame. A dropped frame immediately doubles the effective observation interval between samples. Downstream state estimators must treat the missing update as an age or sequence fault rather than assuming that fresh scene geometry will arrive on schedule.

The underlying microarchitectural mechanisms governing frame delivery (DMA rings, IOMMU mappings, and memory controller arbitration) are treated systematically by @hennessy2019computer and @bryant2015computer. For physical AI systems, the essential design metric is capture-to-consumer age and its tail distribution under the intended camera workload.

Delivering an on-time frame establishes only when the physical scene was sampled. Determining where objects reside within that frame, and bounding the uncertainty of that spatial estimate, introduces geometric and calibration errors that consume the remainder of the safety clearance envelope.

## Spatial Error and Clearance Bounds {#sec-perception-error-clearance}

If perception places a warehouse rack upright just a few centimeters farther from the base's trajectory than it actually stands, the motion planner consumes those missing centimeters directly from its `{python} RollingShutterSkew.side_clearance_str` side clearance, although no stage of the pipeline decided to spend them. Once downstream control logic uses an estimated coordinate to authorize motion, every spatial error becomes a physical displacement drawn from the clearance that protects the robot from collision. Transforming a raw sensor observation into a trustworthy clearance claim requires **metric grounding**\index{Metric grounding!definition}, which maps detector measurements into Euclidean space. This grounding relies on unprojecting two-dimensional sensor measurements into three dimensions, an inverse problem that assumes calibrated optics, rigid structural mountings, and predictable surface properties.

Classical projective geometry and triangulation [@hartley2003multiple; @szeliski2022computer] govern how measurement noise converts into three-dimensional spatial displacement. In two-view streaming perception, two calibrated cameras with optical centers $\CameraOpticalCenter_1, \CameraOpticalCenter_2$ observe a physical scene point $\CartesianPosition \in \mathbb{R}^3$. The baseline vector $\RigidTransformTranslation \in \mathbb{R}^3$ connecting $\CameraOpticalCenter_1$ and $\CameraOpticalCenter_2$, together with the target point $\CartesianPosition$, defines the **epipolar plane**\index{Epipolar geometry!epipolar plane}. The intersection of this baseline with each image plane defines the two **epipoles** $\ImageEpipole_1, \ImageEpipole_2$.

For corresponding image coordinates $\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_1, \HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_2$ expressed in homogeneous pixel coordinates, the rigid spatial transformation $(\DirectionalCosineMatrix, \RigidTransformTranslation) \in \text{SE}(3)$ relating the camera frames establishes the fundamental **epipolar constraint**\index{Epipolar constraint!definition}:
$$\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_2^\top \FundamentalMatrix \, \HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_1 = 0$$
where $\FundamentalMatrix = \CameraIntrinsicInverseTranspose_2 \EssentialMatrix \, \CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix_1^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is the **Fundamental matrix**\index{Fundamental matrix}, and $\EssentialMatrix = [\RigidTransformTranslation]_\times \DirectionalCosineMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ is the **Essential matrix**\index{Essential matrix} (with $[\RigidTransformTranslation]_\times$ denoting the skew-symmetric matrix of baseline translation). The vector $\EpipolarLine_2 = \FundamentalMatrix \HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_1$ defines the **epipolar line** in the second image; any valid physical correspondence $\HomogeneousPixelCoordinates_2$ must lie strictly along $\EpipolarLine_2$.

In a calibrated **rectified stereo rig**\index{Stereo rectification!epipolar lines}, both images are digitally warped onto a shared virtual image plane parallel to the baseline ($\DirectionalCosineMatrix = \IdentityMatrix$, $\RigidTransformTranslation = [\StereoBaseline, 0, 0]^\top$). Rectification forces epipolar lines to be exactly parallel and collinear with horizontal pixel scanlines ($\PixelRowCoordinate_1 = \PixelRowCoordinate_2$). This geometric transformation collapses an expensive two-dimensional correspondence search, the kind dense optical-flow networks perform, into a one-dimensional search along the same horizontal scanline. Neural stereo networks such as RAFT-Stereo evaluate this correspondence as a 1D correlation cost volume [@lipson2021raftstereo]: disparity is simply the horizontal coordinate difference $\StereoDisparity = \PixelColumnCoordinate_1 - \PixelColumnCoordinate_2$, recovering metric depth through $\CameraFrameDepth = \frac{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline}{\StereoDisparity}$.

When mechanical vibration, chassis twist, or thermal expansion induces uncalibrated relative pitch or roll between cameras, or when rolling-shutter readout shears scanlines during sharp platform turns, the true physical correspondence shifts vertically off the horizontal epipolar line ($\FiniteChange \PixelRowCoordinate \neq 0$). The 1D correlation cost volume fails or latches onto spurious texture matches across adjacent rows, injecting severe triangulation outliers into the reconstruction. Differentiating the unprojection $\CameraFrameDepth = \frac{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline}{\StereoDisparity}$ with respect to disparity yields a negative signed derivative whose magnitude defines the small-error relation (@eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty):
$$|\SmallPerturbation \CameraFrameDepth| \approx \frac{\CameraFrameDepth^2}{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline} |\SmallPerturbation \StereoDisparity|$$ {#eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty}
where $\SmallPerturbation \StereoDisparity$ represents disparity error. If $\SmallPerturbation \StereoDisparity$ denotes a disparity standard deviation $\DisparityStandardDeviation$, first-order error propagation gives $\DepthStandardDeviation \approx \frac{\CameraFrameDepth^2}{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline}\DisparityStandardDeviation$. Doubling range quadruples this modeled standard deviation at fixed focal length $\FocalLength$, baseline $\StereoBaseline$, and disparity precision $\DisparityStandardDeviation$. For distant landmarks, an estimator instead parameterizes depth as inverse depth[^fn-inverse-depth-parametrization] $\InverseDepth = 1/\CameraFrameDepth = \StereoDisparity / (\FocalLength \StereoBaseline)$. Differentiating inverse depth with respect to disparity yields:
$$\frac{\partial \InverseDepth}{\partial \StereoDisparity} = \frac{1}{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline} = \text{constant}$$
Because this derivative is independent of distance, measurement errors in disparity map linearly into inverse depth ($\SmallPerturbation \InverseDepth = \frac{1}{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline} \SmallPerturbation \StereoDisparity$). This linear mapping provides **inverse-depth metric grounding**\index{Inverse-depth metric grounding!definition}, preserving numerical conditioning for distant landmarks when the disparity-error model is appropriate. Inverse depth does not eliminate mismatch outliers or guarantee estimator stability. In contrast, a pulsed time-of-flight sensor estimates range directly from transit time, $\RadialRange = \frac{\VacuumLightSpeed \PulseRoundTripTime}{2}$; its range error depends on its timing and detection electronics, remaining approximately flat across its rated operating region.

[^fn-inverse-depth-parametrization]: **Inverse-Depth Parametrization**\index{Mathematics!inverse-depth}: @civera2008inverse introduced it for monocular SLAM, where a newly seen landmark may lie arbitrarily far away. Storing $\InverseDepth = 1/\CameraFrameDepth$ lets a point at infinity enter the estimate as $\InverseDepth = 0$ with finite variance, where a depth coordinate would need an infinite one, so near and distant landmarks share one well-conditioned representation. The full parameterization is given in @sec-appendix-ml-spatial.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-stereo-depth-error
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STEREO DEPTH-ERROR SCALE AND BASELINE THERMAL BIAS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The stereo worked example of @sec-perception-error-clearance and
# │          the thermal-expansion footnote of @sec-perception-observation-contract.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how the one-sigma stereo depth scale grows with squared range,
# │          why adding it to a clearance kept along the viewing ray does not
# │          give an inset, and
# │          what an unmodeled baseline change does to depth at long range.
# │ Show:    sigma_z 12.5 mm at 2 m and 312.5 mm at 10 m; a 150 mm ray clearance plus
# │          one sigma 162.5 mm and 462.5 mm; 10 mm depth bias at 20 m.
# │ How:     sigma_z = z^2 sigma_d / (f b); |dz| = z |db| / b.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_display_math, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class StereoDepthError:
    """One-sigma stereo depth scale on an illustrative rig, and baseline thermal bias."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    b = 0.20 * meter  # category: illustrative (stereo baseline)
    f_px = 800.0  # category: illustrative (focal length, pixels)
    sigma_d_px = 0.5  # category: illustrative (disparity standard deviation, pixels)
    z_near = 2.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    z_far = 10.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    db = 0.1 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (unmodeled baseline change)
    z_thermal = 20.0 * meter  # category: illustrative
    c_ray = 150.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (clearance kept along the viewing ray)
    z_rack = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative (localization allowance)
    side_clearance = AISLE.side_clearance  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    sigma_z_near = (z_near**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(millimeter)
    sigma_z_far = (z_far**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(millimeter)
    naive_near = (c_ray + sigma_z_near).to(millimeter)
    naive_far = (c_ray + sigma_z_far).to(millimeter)
    dz_thermal = (z_thermal * db / b).to(millimeter)
    sigma_z_rack = (z_rack**2 * sigma_d_px / (f_px * b)).to(millimeter)
    z_star_loc = ((delta_loc * f_px * b / sigma_d_px) ** 0.5).to(meter)  # range where sigma_z = delta_loc
    z_star_side = ((side_clearance * f_px * b / sigma_d_px) ** 0.5).to(meter)  # range where sigma_z = side clearance
    z_star_side_half_b = ((side_clearance * f_px * (b / 2) / sigma_d_px) ** 0.5).to(meter)  # checkpoint: halved baseline

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(sigma_z_near.magnitude - 12.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected near sigma_z: {sigma_z_near}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_far.magnitude - 312.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected far sigma_z: {sigma_z_far}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_far / sigma_z_near - 25.0) < 1e-9, "Depth scale must grow with squared range")
    check(abs(dz_thermal.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected thermal depth bias: {dz_thermal}")
    check(abs(sigma_z_rack.magnitude - 3.78) < 0.01, f"Unexpected sigma_z at the rack end: {sigma_z_rack}")
    check(abs(z_star_loc.magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected delta_loc crossover range: {z_star_loc}")
    check(abs(z_star_side.magnitude - 6.93) < 0.005, f"Unexpected side-clearance crossover range: {z_star_side}")
    check(z_rack < z_star_loc < z_star_side < z_far, "Notebook says the rack end sits well inside both crossovers")
    check(abs(z_star_side_half_b.magnitude - 4.90) < 0.005, f"Checkpoint answer drifted: {z_star_side_half_b}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    b_str = fmt_length(b, unit=meter, precision=2)
    f_px_str = fmt(f_px, precision=0)
    sigma_d_px_str = fmt(sigma_d_px, precision=1)
    z_near_str = fmt_length(z_near, unit=meter, precision=0)
    z_far_str = fmt_length(z_far, unit=meter, precision=0)
    sigma_z_near_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_near, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    sigma_z_far_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_far, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    c_ray_str = fmt_length(c_ray, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    naive_near_str = fmt_length(naive_near, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    naive_far_str = fmt_length(naive_far, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    db_str = fmt_length(db, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    z_thermal_str = fmt_length(z_thermal, unit=meter, precision=0)
    dz_thermal_str = fmt_length(dz_thermal, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    z_rack_str = fmt_length(z_rack.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    delta_loc_str = fmt_length(delta_loc.to(millimeter), unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    side_clearance_str = fmt_length(side_clearance.to(meter), unit=meter, precision=2)
    sigma_z_rack_str = fmt_length(sigma_z_rack, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    z_star_loc_str = fmt_length(z_star_loc, unit=meter, precision=0)
    z_star_side_str = fmt_length(z_star_side, unit=meter, precision=1)

    # Display arithmetic for nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall (magnitudes, LaTeX units)
    _fb = fmt(f_px * b.to(meter).magnitude, precision=0)  # f b in pixel-meters
    _sd = fmt(sigma_d_px, precision=1)
    _zn = fmt(z_near.to(meter).magnitude, precision=0)
    _zf = fmt(z_far.to(meter).magnitude, precision=0)
    _ratio = fmt((sigma_z_far / sigma_z_near).to(dimensionless).magnitude, precision=0)
    _loc = fmt(delta_loc.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)
    _side = fmt(side_clearance.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)
    sigma_rack_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\sigma_z = \frac{{z^2 \sigma_d}}{{f b}} = \frac{{({fmt(z_rack.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)}\ \text{{m}})^2 \times {_sd}\ \text{{px}}}}{{{f_px_str}\ \text{{px}} \times {fmt(b.to(meter).magnitude, precision=2)}\ \text{{m}}}} = {fmt(sigma_z_rack.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad \frac{{\sigma_z({_zf}\ \text{{m}})}}{{\sigma_z({_zn}\ \text{{m}})}} = \frac{{{fmt(sigma_z_far.magnitude, precision=1)}}}{{{fmt(sigma_z_near.magnitude, precision=1)}}} = {_ratio}"
    )
    crossover_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"z^{{*}} = \sqrt{{\frac{{C\,f b}}{{\sigma_d}}}}: \quad \sqrt{{\frac{{{_loc}\ \text{{m}} \times {_fb}\ \text{{px}}\cdot\text{{m}}}}{{{_sd}\ \text{{px}}}}}} = {fmt(z_star_loc.magnitude, precision=0)}\ \text{{m}}, \quad \sqrt{{\frac{{{_side}\ \text{{m}} \times {_fb}\ \text{{px}}\cdot\text{{m}}}}{{{_sd}\ \text{{px}}}}}} = {fmt(z_star_side.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{m}}"
    )
```

On the running machine, the rack-end range comes from the OS1-64 LiDAR, whose datasheet quotes one-standard-deviation precision of `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_min_str` to `{python} LidarSweep.sigma_r_max_str` beyond 1 m in the 1024×10 Hz mode. Applying that scale to the selected scan mode requires bias and residual-tail qualification under the intended surfaces and motion. A design that tried to range with cameras alone would have to triangulate, because the navigation camera by itself recovers only the bearing ray of @eq-percep-bearing-ray. An illustrative stereo pair shows where such a design meets a range wall, by asking how far down the aisle its depth error stays inside the stopping budget's allowances. Notebook \ref{nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall} evaluates @eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty on that rig, and @fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance plots the curve.

::: {#nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall .callout-notebook title="The stereo range wall"}

**Problem**: An illustrative stereo pair must place a rack upright for the base's clearance checks. How large is its one-standard-deviation depth scale at the rack end, and at what range does that scale alone consume the localization allowance and then the whole side clearance?

**Variables**:

* Baseline $\StereoBaseline =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str`, focal length $\FocalLength =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.f_px_str` px, and disparity standard deviation $\DisparityStandardDeviation =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_d_px_str` px over the tested range (Illustrative rig; the running machine carries no depth camera).
* Rack-end range $\CameraFrameDepth =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.z_rack_str` (Illustrative).
* Allowances $\ClearanceAllowance$: localization $\LocalizationBound =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.delta_loc_str` and side clearance `{python} StereoDepthError.side_clearance_str` (Illustrative; @sec-appendix-systems-machine-data-sheet).

**Math**:

*Depth scale.* At the rack end, and between the figure's two quoted ranges,
`{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_rack_math`

*Crossover ranges.* Setting $\DepthStandardDeviation$ equal to an allowance $\ClearanceAllowance$ and solving for range,
`{python} StereoDepthError.crossover_math`

*Sensitivity.* Five times the range costs twenty-five times the depth scale, so the crossovers move only with the square root of $\FocalLength \StereoBaseline / \DisparityStandardDeviation$.

**Result**: At the rack end, one standard deviation is `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_rack_str`. It equals $\LocalizationBound$ at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_loc_str` and the whole side clearance at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_side_str`.

**Systems insight**: Stereo depth error is a range budget. This rig's nominal depth scale fits the rack-end allowance, but supporting that decision still requires the tail, bias, and timing qualification developed below. A claim about an obstacle several meters down the aisle spends the stopping budget's $\LocalizationBound$ on one standard deviation alone, so beyond a few meters the clearance claim must come from a range sensor whose error does not grow with $\CameraFrameDepth^2$, or the speed must fall.

:::

The values in Notebook \ref{nbk-perception-stereo-range-wall} are nominal **one-standard-deviation scales**, not clearance insets or certified 99th-percentile bounds. A usable safety inset requires an empirical tail quantile of the *full spatial residual*, calibrated on the intended sensor across realistic range, surface texture, platform motion, and ambient lighting conditions, with systematic bias and missed detections handled separately.

A pervasive trap in visual estimation is assuming that measurement errors follow a nominal Gaussian distribution where a $3\MeasurementErrorStandardDeviation$ gate bounds 99.7 percent of all errors. In physical vision, disparity estimation relies on matching pixel appearance across views. When scenes contain repetitive textures (such as corrugated warehouse siding), specular reflections from polished concrete floors, or partial occlusions along object silhouettes, correspondence matching produces catastrophic multimodal outliers rather than Gaussian scatter. A fraction of stereo returns are then gross mismatch outliers lying many standard deviations from the true surface. Because that outlier fraction depends on scene texture, lighting, and the matching architecture, it must be measured directly on residuals from operational deployments rather than assumed. Relying on Gaussian $3\MeasurementErrorStandardDeviation$ bounds without robust loss formulations (such as Huber or Tukey loss) or heavy-tailed empirical quantile validation allows these gross outliers to distort the state estimate, directly compromising physical clearance. When validated range-error bounds exceed stopping margins, the vehicle must reduce speed or refuse the motion proposal entirely.

### Clearance inset margins and transform chain propagation

Spatial error extends well beyond the sensor's optical frame. Before an estimated point can govern motion, it must propagate through kinematic coordinate transformations into the robot base frame and end effector. The mechanics of rigid body transformations\index{Rigid body transformations} and SE(3) kinematic frame composition\index{SE(3) kinematics} follow classical treatments by Craig [@craig2005introduction] and @lynch2017modern. Each link in this transform chain contributes scale errors, mounting calibration drift, joint encoder quantization, and mechanical compliance under load (such as a robot arm sagging under gravitational torque). As demonstrated by the reference-frame principles of @sec-perception-handoff, angular misalignment at the sensor mount amplifies linearly with range. If the navigation camera's extrinsic calibration shifts by $\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_ext_str` rad against the chassis, the lateral error $\SmallPerturbation \CartesianXCoordinate \approx \CameraFrameDepth\,\ExtrinsicMisalignmentAngle$ at $\CameraFrameDepth =$ `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.z_ext_str` reaches `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dx_ext_str`. The shift is lateral, so on the approach to the rack end it is charged against the side clearance, as the readout notebook charged lateral skew. Its size is the point, because it is as large as the entire `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.delta_loc_str` allowance $\LocalizationBound$ that the stopping budget holds for localization along the direction of travel.

The comparison therefore concerns error scale rather than which allowance pays. The localization allowance carries small, validated residuals, such as the sub-millimeter travel during the clock-conversion bound that the observation contract absorbs (@sec-perception-observation-contract). An extrinsic shift that consumes that entire budget represents a mechanical calibration failure; downstream consumers must detect and refuse such observations via calibration validity checks rather than absorb them. When combined with quadratic stereo depth dispersion, the total spatial error vector $\SpatialErrorVector$ at standoff range is anisotropic: it is dominated by longitudinal depth along the optical axis and angular lever-arm effects orthogonal to it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How the localization allowance enters the base's kinetic barrier certificate is developed in @sec-enforcement-kinetic-barrier-certificates.
:::

Every physical safety barrier operates by defending a geometric boundary around the machine envelope. For a spatial position error vector $\SpatialErrorVector$, the triangle inequality gives a conservative relation between nominal and true clearance:
$$\TrueClearance \ge \NominalClearance - \|\SpatialErrorVector\|$$
To ensure the true obstacle remains beyond the required safe physical clearance $\RequiredClearance$ (such as the base's side clearance), the permission path enforces a clearance inset $\ClearanceInset$ (@eq-percep-clearance-inset):
$$\ClearanceInset = \RequiredClearance + \|\SpatialErrorVector\|_{\text{p99}}$$ {#eq-percep-clearance-inset}
Here $\|\SpatialErrorVector\|_{\text{p99}}$ is an empirically certified 99th-percentile quantile of the full spatial residual norm, incorporating optical noise, kinematic propagation, and uncalibrated mounting bias. The tempting shortcut replaces that quantile with one standard deviation from the stereo notebook. For a required clearance of $\RequiredClearance =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.c_ray_str`, it would hold an inset of `{python} StereoDepthError.naive_near_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_near_str` or `{python} StereoDepthError.naive_far_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_far_str`, and neither number covers the Gaussian tail beyond one standard deviation or the mismatch outliers described earlier. The measured quantile targets 99 percent coverage under the declared calibration assumptions; it does not provide a hard bound on the remaining residual tail. Closing that residual tail requires a justified hard bound on the sensing error, a feasible stopping trajectory, and a safety filter that responds within the remaining latency margin.

::: {#dfn-perception-clearance-inset .callout-definition title="Clearance inset"}

***Clearance inset***\index{Clearance inset!definition} ($\ClearanceInset$) is the separation a consumer holds between an estimated obstacle position and the machine's envelope so that the true obstacle stays at least the required physical clearance away, except with a stated tail probability measured under the conditions of use.

1.  **Significance**: The inset converts measured spatial error into clearance that the motion gives up (@eq-percep-clearance-inset). Every millimeter of qualified error widens the region the permission path treats as occupied, so the planner must slow or route farther away. On the illustrative stereo rig, one standard deviation of depth error alone equals the base's `{python} StereoDepthError.side_clearance_str` side clearance at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_side_str`, so there the inset would double the clearance even if the residual tail were no wider than one standard deviation.
2.  **Distinction**: A covariance describes the second moments of the error an estimator believes it has; the inset rests on residuals measured against ground truth, so it includes the bias and heavy tail that the covariance omits. A 99th-percentile inset is also not a hard bound: it leaves 1 percent of residuals outside, whose containment requires a justified sensing-error bound, a feasible response under that bound, and a timely independent permission path. A stop calculated from the same unsupported observation does not independently cover its residual tail.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a reported covariance, or a depth network's predicted spread, sets the inset. Neither is measured against ground truth, so neither contains the calibration bias and mismatch outliers that the residual campaign of @sec-perception-qualifying-error captures.

:::

The two halves of the argument sit side by side in @fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance. The stereo depth scale climbs quadratically past the LiDAR's flat datasheet precision for the specified 1024×10 Hz mode, and the inset holds the estimate far enough out that only the measured residual tail, which unmodeled bias can enlarge, falls inside $\RequiredClearance$.

::: {#fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Depth error scale and clearance inset**: (a) For the illustrative stereo rig, the one-standard-deviation depth scale grows with squared range, from `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_near_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_near_str` to `{python} StereoDepthError.sigma_z_far_str` at `{python} StereoDepthError.z_far_str`; the gray band is the OS1-64 datasheet range precision beyond 1 m in the specified 1024×10 Hz mode. Its transfer to the selected operating mode requires residual qualification. (b) A schematic error distribution along the viewing ray. Holding the estimate at $\ClearanceInset = \RequiredClearance + \|\SpatialErrorVector\|_{\text{p99}}$ keeps the true surface beyond $\RequiredClearance$ except in the shaded residual tail, which the quantile leaves and which bias can enlarge." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. Top: a line plot of one-sigma depth error in millimeters against range in meters, a curve rising quadratically with two marked points at 2 and 10 meters, above a flat gray band for OS1 datasheet precision at 1024 by 10 hertz. Bottom: a schematic bell-shaped distribution with heavy tails along a distance axis with ticks for body, C safe, and C inset; the estimate sits at the dashed C inset line, an arrow between C safe and C inset is labeled with the 99th-percentile error norm, and the small part of the distribution closer than C safe is shaded red and labeled residual tail and bias."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-perception-depth-clearance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DEPTH ERROR SCALE AND CLEARANCE INSET (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-08-depth-uncertainty-clearance in
# │          @sec-perception-error-clearance.
# │
# │ Goal:    Contrast a stereo depth scale that grows with squared range with
# │          OS1-64 datasheet precision at 1024 x 10 Hz, then show what a
# │          validated quantile inset buys and what it leaves.
# │ Show:    (a) sigma_z(z) for the illustrative stereo rig with its two quoted
# │          points, and the OS1-64 precision band; (b) a schematic error
# │          density along the viewing ray with C_safe, the P99 inset, and the
# │          residual tail.
# │ How:     (a) reads StereoDepthError and LidarSweep (no literals); (b) is a
# │          schematic with symbolic ticks only (no plotted numbers).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check
from mlsysim.core.units import millimeter

SDE, LS = StereoDepthError, LidarSweep
PETROL, INK, SOFT, PALE = "#007A87", "#1A202C", "#4A5568", "#A0AEC0"
PINE, CRIMSON = "#1A4D3E", "#A51C30"  # structural, consequence (theme-colors.tex)

# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
k_mm_per_m2 = (SDE.sigma_d_px / (SDE.f_px * SDE.b)).to(millimeter / meter**2).magnitude  # category: derived
z_far_m = SDE.z_far.to(meter).magnitude
z_near_m = SDE.z_near.to(meter).magnitude
lid_lo = LS.sigma_r_min.to(millimeter).magnitude  # category: datasheet
lid_hi = LS.sigma_r_max.to(millimeter).magnitude  # category: datasheet

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
z = np.linspace(0.0, 1.2 * z_far_m, 200)
sig = k_mm_per_m2 * z**2

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2 - SDE.sigma_z_far.to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Plotted stereo curve must pass through sigma_z_far.")
check(abs(k_mm_per_m2 * z_near_m**2 - SDE.sigma_z_near.to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Plotted stereo curve must pass through sigma_z_near.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 5.8), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.45))

# (a) depth error scale
ax.axhspan(lid_lo, lid_hi, xmin=1.0 / (1.2 * z_far_m), color=PALE, alpha=0.45, lw=0)
ax.text(
    1.2 * z_far_m * 0.98,
    lid_hi + 10,
    f"OS1 1024×10 Hz\n$\\sigma_R$: {LS.sigma_r_min_str} to {LS.sigma_r_max_str}",
    ha="right",
    va="bottom",
    fontsize=9,
    color=SOFT,
)
ax.plot(z, sig, color=PETROL, lw=1.8)
for zz, s_str in ((z_near_m, SDE.sigma_z_near_str), (z_far_m, SDE.sigma_z_far_str)):
    ax.plot([zz], [k_mm_per_m2 * zz**2], "o", color=PETROL, ms=4)
ax.annotate(
    f"{SDE.sigma_z_far_str} at {SDE.z_far_str}",
    xy=(z_far_m, k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2),
    xytext=(z_far_m * 0.18, k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2 * 1.05),
    fontsize=9,
    color=PETROL,
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PALE, lw=0.6),
)
ax.annotate(
    f"{SDE.sigma_z_near_str} at {SDE.z_near_str}",
    xy=(z_near_m, k_mm_per_m2 * z_near_m**2),
    xytext=(z_near_m * 0.55, k_mm_per_m2 * z_far_m**2 * 0.42),
    fontsize=9,
    color=PETROL,
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PALE, lw=0.6),
)
ax.text(z_far_m * 0.62, k_mm_per_m2 * (z_far_m * 1.1) ** 2, r"stereo $\sigma_z \propto Z_c^2$", fontsize=9, color=PETROL, ha="right", va="center")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.2 * z_far_m)
ax.set_ylim(0, k_mm_per_m2 * (1.2 * z_far_m) ** 2 * 1.02)
ax.set_xlabel("range $Z_c$ (m)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("one-sigma depth error (mm)", fontsize=9)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=9)
ax.set_title("(a)", fontsize=9, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
for s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)

# (b) schematic: error density along the viewing ray, heavy tailed
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 600)
c_safe, c_inset = 3.4, 6.0
dens = (1 + ((x - c_inset) / 0.8) ** 2 / 2.0) ** (-1.5)
bx.fill_between(x, 0, dens, where=x >= c_safe, color=PETROL, alpha=0.18, lw=0)
bx.fill_between(x, 0, dens, where=x <= c_safe, color=CRIMSON, alpha=0.35, lw=0)
bx.plot(x, dens, color=PETROL, lw=1.3)
bx.axvline(c_safe, color=PINE, lw=1.2)
bx.axvline(c_inset, color=PINE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 3)))
bx.text(c_inset + 0.1, 1.1, "estimate held\nat the inset", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=SOFT)
bx.annotate("", xy=(c_safe, 0.86), xytext=(c_inset, 0.86), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=PINE, lw=0.9))
bx.text((c_safe + c_inset) / 2, 0.9, "$\\|\\,\\epsilon\\,\\|_{\\mathrm{p99}}$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=PINE)
bx.annotate("", xy=(0, 0.62), xytext=(c_safe, 0.62), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=PINE, lw=0.9))
bx.text(c_safe / 2, 0.66, "$C_{\\mathrm{safe}}$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=9, color=PINE)
bx.annotate(
    "residual tail\nand bias",
    xy=(c_safe - 0.5, 0.05),
    xytext=(c_safe - 0.4, 0.34),
    ha="right",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=CRIMSON,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=CRIMSON, lw=0.6),
)
bx.set_xticks([0, c_safe, c_inset])
bx.set_xticklabels(["body", "$C_{\\mathrm{safe}}$", "$C_{\\mathrm{inset}}$"], fontsize=9)
bx.set_yticks([])
bx.set_xlim(0, 10)
bx.set_ylim(0, 1.3)
bx.set_xlabel("distance along the viewing ray", fontsize=9)
bx.grid(False)
bx.set_title("(b)", fontsize=9, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
for s in ("top", "right", "left"):
    bx.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

:::

Because clearance depends on propagated spatial error, downstream motion planners and safety arbitration layers cannot consume raw coordinate tuples. A covariance matrix $\BodyFramePointCovariance \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ alone cannot determine whether a $10\ \text{mm}$ or $500\ \text{mm}$ clearance inset is justified; establishing that buffer requires an independently validated tail quantile or hard bound.

When spatial error is qualified, the permission path can expand the clearance inset, trading speed or workspace for separation. Downstream deterministic safety filters, the per-tick checks that keep the machine inside a region from which it can still stop, hold it outside this expanded boundary $\ClearanceInset$ and so preserve the clearance buffer against sensing and calibration error. Environmental hazards such as a textureless wall, solar glare, or lost calibration can invalidate that qualification without making a numerical covariance matrix literally infinite. The permission path must then refuse motion proposals that depend on the affected claim and select a feasible fallback.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Safety filters, and the control barrier functions that formalize them, are developed in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

On every frame, the producer builds a spatial claim in a fixed order, where any failed check halts the pipeline. It first converts the capture timestamp to the consumer's clock with a bounded synchronization error and computes the observation age $\DispatchObservationAge$ at dispatch. If age plus clock uncertainty exceeds the dispatch threshold, it marks the observation stale, and proposals that need it are refused. At admission and across subsequent ticks, the permission path computes the current evidence age relative to capture time and compares it with a separate, later runtime staleness threshold (@sec-perception-observation-contract). For a fresh observation, the producer unprojects each pixel measurement into optical coordinates with a sensor covariance,[^fn-covariance-unprojection-depth] and carries point and covariance into the body frame by first-order SE(3) error propagation\index{SE(3) kinematics!error propagation} through the calibrated extrinsics at capture. A consumer that predicts forward must attach its motion-model uncertainty without altering the evidence epoch. Validated residuals, including bias, then set the inset radius $\ClearanceInset$, and when no valid bound remains, the affected motion is refused. What leaves perception is an error-qualified claim $(\BodyFramePoint, \BodyFramePointCovariance, \ClearanceInset, \DispatchObservationAge)$, never a bare coordinate.

[^fn-covariance-unprojection-depth]: **Covariance Propagation**\index{Mathematics!covariance propagation}: First-order propagation maps measurement covariance to $\CameraFramePointCovariance = \UnprojectionJacobian\MeasurementNoiseCovariance\UnprojectionJacobian^\top$ in the optical frame and then to $\BodyFramePointCovariance = \CameraExtrinsicRotation\CameraFramePointCovariance\CameraExtrinsicRotation^\top + \ExtrinsicCalibrationCovariance$ in the body frame, where the extrinsic term is what a mount shift adds. Its largest eigenvalue gives the principal variance scale, which for stereo points lies along the viewing ray; @sec-appendix-systems-vision derives the full propagation.

That claim describes one measurement at one instant, and perception's responsibility ends with it. Keeping the rack-end range current between sweeps, fusing the LiDAR with a second sensor, joining detections into tracks, and applying a late measurement at its capture epoch are estimation over time. @Sec-memory takes them up, beginning with state estimation in @sec-perception-state-estimation, and every one of them consumes the dated, framed, error-qualified claim built here. What perception must still supply is evidence that the claimed error was measured.

### Qualifying the claimed error {#sec-perception-qualifying-error}

Two numbers in the claim just built cannot come from a model or a datasheet: the tail quantile that sets the clearance inset, and the clock-conversion bound that dates the claim on the permission path's clock. Each is fixed by a measurement campaign, and the observation contract of @sec-perception-observation-contract carries both. Whether a reported covariance matches empirical error is evaluated with consistency statistics that require an estimator's prediction; that test is developed alongside the estimator (@sec-memory-estimator-consistency).

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-error-qualification
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TAIL-QUANTILE AND CLOCK-DRIFT QUALIFICATION NUMBERS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-perception-qualifying-error.
# │
# │ Goal:    Give the conformal rank for a 99th-percentile bound and the drift
# │          of a free-running sensor clock between syncs.
# │ Show:    at least 99 residuals for a 1 percent bound; with 1,000, the 991st
# │          smallest (10th largest); 10 us of drift.
# │ How:     split-conformal rank ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha)); Ouster OS1 Rev7
# │          internal clock drift (10 ppm) over a chosen 1 s sync interval.
# │          The covariance-consistency bands moved with the estimator to
# │          @sec-memory-estimator-consistency.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_int, fmt_latency, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ErrorQualification:
    """Sample sizes for a clearance-inset quantile and the clock-drift bound."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    alpha = 0.01  # category: chosen (tail mass for the clearance inset)
    n_resid = 1000  # category: chosen (calibration residuals)
    drift_ppm = RM.lidar.internal_clock_drift.to(ppm).magnitude  # category: datasheet (registry: OS1 Rev7 internal clock drift)
    t_sync = 1.0 * second  # category: chosen (sync interval)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_min = math.ceil((1 - alpha) / alpha)
    k_rank = math.ceil((n_resid + 1) * (1 - alpha))
    k_from_top = n_resid - k_rank + 1
    drift = (drift_ppm * 1e-6 * t_sync).to(microsecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_min == 99, f"Unexpected minimum calibration size: {n_min}")
    check(k_rank == 991 and k_from_top == 10, f"Unexpected conformal rank: {k_rank}")
    check(abs(drift.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected clock drift: {drift}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_pct_str = fmt_percent(alpha, precision=0, style="prose")
    n_min_str = fmt_int(n_min)
    n_resid_str = fmt_int(n_resid, commas=True)
    k_rank_str = fmt_int(k_rank)
    k_from_top_str = fmt_int(k_from_top)
    drift_ppm_str = fmt(drift_ppm, precision=0)
    t_sync_str = fmt(t_sync.to(second).magnitude, precision=0)
    drift_str = fmt_latency(drift, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
```

The clearance inset of @eq-percep-clearance-inset needs a 99th-percentile bound on the residual norm under intended operational conditions, not a theoretical covariance. The most direct procedure is empirical. Collect $\CalibrationExampleCount$ residual norms against ground truth, sort them, and select the $\ConformalQuantileRank$-th smallest with $\ConformalQuantileRank = \lceil (\CalibrationExampleCount+1)(1-\ConformalMiscoverageRate) \rceil$. This split-conformal rule guarantees that a future residual falls at or below the bound with probability at least $1 - \ConformalMiscoverageRate$, provided calibration and deployment residuals are exchangeable [@angelopoulos2023gentle]. It is the inductive conformal construction that @sec-brain-softmax-illusion used to turn a policy's dispersion into a coverage guarantee, applied here to measured residual norms rather than to model scores. For $\ConformalMiscoverageRate =$ `{python} ErrorQualification.alpha_pct_str`, the rule requires at least `{python} ErrorQualification.n_min_str` residuals, returning the largest observed value when evaluated on that minimum set. With `{python} ErrorQualification.n_resid_str` residuals, it returns the `{python} ErrorQualification.k_rank_str`st smallest value (the `{python} ErrorQualification.k_from_top_str`th largest). This guarantee holds marginally over the calibration distribution. A new floor finish, a lighting change, or a mechanical recalibration breaks exchangeability, requiring new residual campaigns sized by the per-claim sample-size rule of @sec-evaluation-trials-per-claim. Because these residuals are measured directly against ground truth, they capture the sensor's physical bias, which nominal covariance models omit.

The synchronization uncertainty bound $\ClockConversionBound$ in the contract is likewise measured rather than assumed. The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) exchange that @sec-data-hw-vs-sw-timestamps used to pair logged frames with actions estimates a device's clock offset by assuming that both directions of the path take equal time [@ieee15882019]. A path asymmetry $\PathDelayAsymmetry$ shifts the estimated offset by $\PathDelayAsymmetry/2$ and leaves no symptom in the exchange, which is why the exchange must be timestamped in hardware at the network interface, where host scheduling cannot add delay to one direction and not the other. Between synchronization exchanges, the local oscillator drifts. The OS1-64's free-running clock is specified at `{python} ErrorQualification.drift_ppm_str` ppm [@ouster2025os1], which over a `{python} ErrorQualification.t_sync_str` s sync interval accumulates `{python} ErrorQualification.drift_str` of worst-case drift. Clock qualification records the measured tail of the servo's reported offset, the path-asymmetry allowance, and the drift between corrections. A sampled tail is statistical evidence, not a maximum-error guarantee; a contract that treats synchronization error as a hard bound also needs a justified limit on unobserved offset excursions and a detector that invalidates the mapping when its assumptions fail. For a hardware-triggered camera, this bound is verified by timing the trigger edge against the IMU latch with a logic analyzer. Until those measurements exist, the clock-conversion bound in the navigation camera's record remains illustrative, and the LiDAR's datasheet guarantees only `{python} LidarAge.eps_ptp_str`.

### Learned depth as a measurement

Learned models add two capabilities to metric perception: a semantic classification of spatial regions, and a depth estimate from a camera that physically measures only bearing. Lifting labeled detections into a persistent, object-centric scene graph carries state across frames, and @sec-memory-hierarchical-scene-graphs develops the maintenance of that graph. Perception must settle a narrower systems question: whether a learned depth estimate may enter a safety clearance claim at all. The semantic layer identifies candidate objects and contacts; the metric layer must establish their physical geometry. Point clouds supply measured surface samples where pulses reflect, but missing returns never prove free space. Persistent representations that retain geometric evidence cannot alter an observation's capture timestamp or convert a learned model score into an error bound.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The volumetric maps that retain this geometric evidence across frames are developed in @sec-memory-volumetric-metric-maps.
:::

Lifting 2D pixel features into 3D metric space requires combining 2D token embeddings with per-pixel depth distributions. In deep monocular depth networks (such as Depth Anything, MiDaS, or metric depth transformers), models predict dense depth maps from monocular visual cues. However, single-view depth estimation is inherently ill-posed due to projective scale ambiguity: an infinite family of physical 3D objects with different scales and distances project to identical pixel arrays. Relative-depth models output scale- or affine-ambiguous predictions, whose conversion to metric depth requires external calibration, represented by $\MetricDepth = \DepthCalibrationScale \cdot \PredictedRelativeDepth + \DepthCalibrationShift$ when the model uses that parameterization. Metric-trained heads directly predict depth in meters, but their units do not certify their error. Both model classes require residual validation and can fail silently on unusual geometries, novel textures, or optical illusions (such as a 2D photograph printed on a flat surface).

In bird's-eye-view (BEV) architectures such as Lift-Splat-Shoot [@philion2020lift], the network predicts a categorical probability distribution over discrete depth bins along each viewing ray. Each 2D feature token is cast outward along its optical sightline ray and 'splatted' into discrete 3D spatial voxel cells weighted by these predicted depth probabilities, transforming disembodied image embeddings into an explicit 3D volumetric representation. The resulting spatial uncertainty ellipsoid deforms non-linearly under perspective unprojection through the unprojection Jacobian $\UnprojectionJacobian = \frac{\partial \CameraFramePoint}{\partial [\PixelColumnCoordinate, \PixelRowCoordinate, \CameraFrameDepth]^\top}$ (@eq-percep-unproj-covariance):
$$\CameraFramePointCovariance = \UnprojectionJacobian \MeasurementNoiseCovariance \UnprojectionJacobian^\top$$ {#eq-percep-unproj-covariance}
While transverse spatial standard deviation expands linearly with range ($\TransverseStandardDeviation \approx \frac{\CameraFrameDepth}{\FocalLength} \PixelStandardDeviation$), stereo radial depth standard deviation expands quadratically ($\DepthStandardDeviation \approx \frac{\CameraFrameDepth^2}{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline} \DisparityStandardDeviation$). This perspective unprojection transforms near-field circular uncertainty disks into highly eccentric, needle-shaped ellipsoids oriented along the camera's sightline, with extreme radial dispersion at long ranges that must be bounded before downstream safety filters can certify clearance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The lift-splat projection of camera features into a metric bird's-eye-view grid is developed in @sec-appendix-ml-bev-lifting.
:::

Because the depth-bin distributions produced by learned lifting stages are uncalibrated model scores rather than certified metric error bounds, the clearance inset of @eq-percep-clearance-inset cannot rest on learned depth alone. Downstream safety enforcers require continuous validation against calibrated active ranging sensors or stereo disparity. This is the division of labor on the running machine. A learned head on the navigation camera may classify the worker and even estimate depth, but the rack-end range that enters the clearance check comes from the LiDAR. The split also keeps the check independent of the proposal it judges, because a checker that consumed the camera's own perception would share every blind spot of the proposer it exists to catch.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The independence a monitor needs from the proposer across sensing, compute, and actuation is developed in @sec-enforcement-where-enforcer-sits.
:::

::: {#psp-perception-metric-veto-invariant .callout-perspective title="The metric veto invariant"}
**Safety is an invariant of metric clearance, not semantic understanding.** When a slow 2 Hz vision-language foundation model classifies a pathway as "clear aisle" or dismisses an object as a harmless shadow, but the `{python} LidarSweep.f_scan_str` LiDAR, or the occupancy grid built from it, detects a physical obstacle return within the stopping envelope, the permission path must honor the qualified occupied-region evidence rather than let semantic confidence erase it. The permission path halts or slows the machine regardless of the semantic model's high confidence. Semantic models propose high-level task goals; qualified metric sensing supplies clearance evidence to the permission path. Neither sensor pipeline itself owns actuator authority.
:::

::: {#chk-percep-clearance-inset .callout-checkpoint title="Spatial error and the clearance inset"}

A spatial claim is spent from the same clearance as its age, and its error must be measured before it is charged.

- [ ] **Quadratic depth error**: Can you explain why stereo depth error grows with the square of range while a pulsed LiDAR's range precision stays roughly flat?
- [ ] **Baseline estimate**: If the illustrative rig's `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str` baseline were halved, at what range would one standard deviation of depth error reach the `{python} StereoDepthError.side_clearance_str` side clearance, compared with `{python} StereoDepthError.z_star_side_str` now?
- [ ] **Covariance vs. clearance inset**: Can you explain why a residual quantile measured against ground truth, not a reported covariance, sets $\ClearanceInset$, and what that quantile still leaves uncovered?
- [ ] **Learned depth vs. metric evidence**: Can you explain why a depth network's predicted spread cannot enter a clearance claim until its residuals are validated, and why qualified metric evidence overrides a semantic label that calls a return a shadow?

:::

Every bound in this section, whether metric, learned, or temporal, assumes that the sensor behaves as calibrated. Propagation bounds the error of a sensor working as modeled; it says nothing about a sensor that has stopped working that way while still delivering frames at its nominal rate.

## Perception Failure Modes and Sensor Degradation {#sec-perception-failure-modes}

A navigation camera can fail in two ways that look entirely different to downstream software. If its serializer link loses lock, the driver raises an error and the frame never arrives. If direct sunlight through an open dock door saturates the lens as the vehicle turns into an aisle, the camera delivers a complete frame at its nominal rate, with a shelving rack hidden under a patch of clipped white pixels. Perception failures divide along this boundary into two operational classes. **Detectable faults**\index{Detectable faults} occur when the physical sensor or communication transport asserts an explicit hardware or software error condition. Examples include a serializer-deserializer (SerDes) link losing clock synchronization, a cyclic redundancy check (CRC) detecting a corrupted payload, a DMA frame buffer overflowing, or a transport bus timing out. These failures are straightforward to handle: the hardware driver raises a fault flag at the ingestion boundary, downstream consumers drop the corrupted frame, and state estimators expand their uncertainty. Once the age of valid sensor evidence exceeds its configured freshness budget, the permission path rejects motion requests that depend on it and invokes a fallback qualified for the remaining state evidence, actuation authority, and stopping margin. In contrast, **silent failures**\index{Silent failure!definition} occur when the sensor hardware, firmware, and transport bus function without error, delivering a structurally valid tensor whose numerical values misrepresent the physical world.

Physical degradation of the optical channel is a frequent source of silent failure. When bright sunlight enters the aperture, incident photons overwhelm the full-well capacity of the CMOS photodiodes, clamping pixel values at their maximum quantization limit across large patches of the sensor array. This **dynamic range saturation**\index{Dynamic range saturation} destroys local spatial gradients. Downstream feature extractors, optical flow estimators, and stereo disparity algorithms fail because numerical optimization over a uniform flat field yields zero directional gradient, even while the camera driver delivers frames at the full nominal rate. Dimly lit environments trigger the opposite failure mode. When ambient photon flux drops, the discrete, stochastic arrival of photons (**photon shot noise**\index{Photon shot noise}) and the thermal and electrical fluctuations of the readout circuitry (**sensor read noise**\index{Sensor read noise}) dominate the signal. As the signal-to-noise ratio collapses, learned neural backbones begin extracting spurious geometric features from random noise patterns rather than physical obstacle boundaries. Contaminants on the protective lens or dome window, such as water droplets, dust, or grease smudges, act as irregular refractive elements and optical low-pass filters. They attenuate contrast, distort spatial geometry, and mask critical obstacles while the transport stack reports flawless operation.

Timing and transport anomalies can also corrupt an observation silently. If an unshielded physical interface experiences electromagnetic interference, deserializer bit slips (where the hardware drops or duplicates a bit, misaligning the subsequent serial data stream) can alter payload semantics without invalidating standard packet lengths. More dangerous than a dropped packet is an observation stamped with an incorrect capture epoch, because no transport monitor detects the error. If an image sensor captures photons at epoch $\TimeInstant_0$, but a late interrupt handler or an unsynchronized system clock timestamps the resulting memory buffer at $\TimeInstant_0 + \SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant$, the downstream state estimator integrates spatial features under an incorrect body pose. Consider a machine traveling with instantaneous velocity $\Velocity$ and linear acceleration $\LinearAcceleration$ along a given trajectory. When perception suffers an undetected timing desynchronization $\SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant$, the state estimator assigns the detected position of an obstacle to the body coordinates at $\TimeInstant_0 + \SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant$ rather than $\TimeInstant_0$. Over the unmodeled time interval $\SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant$, the physical state estimation error $\FiniteChange \CartesianPosition$ between the asserted position and the true position is governed by the kinematic drift relation (@eq-percep-kinematic-drift):
$$\FiniteChange \CartesianPosition = \Velocity \cdot \SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant + \frac{1}{2} \LinearAcceleration \cdot (\SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant)^2$$ {#eq-percep-kinematic-drift}

The arrival stamp discussed in @sec-perception-handoff represents a silent desynchronization of this exact type. At constant velocity, the acceleration term vanishes, leaving the kinematic offset $\Velocity\,\ArrivalStampOffset$ uncorrected while the driver reports nominal health. The asymmetry between a lost frame and a misdated one needs no estimator mechanics to see. An estimator that accepts a misdated frame as a correctly timed measurement can shrink its reported uncertainty around the wrong position, while a missing update can leave uncertainty to grow under its motion model. In this case, a dropped frame adds no information, so the reported spread grows and the evidence is honestly one frame period (`{python} SensorInformationAge.t_frame_str`) older. A misdated frame is accepted as information, so the spread shrinks around a position offset by $\SpeedAtDetection\,\SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant$. On the running machine the arrival stamp alone places the obstacle `{python} ArrivalStampOffset.dx_recv_str` from where it stood, and the estimator reports that wrong position with more confidence than before, leaving the motion planner sure that it has already cleared an obstacle it is about to strike. @Sec-memory develops the recursive estimator in which this happens, the Kalman filter.

Defending against silent failures requires dedicated runtime health monitors placed directly at the sensor ingestion boundary.
