A pixel-intensity histogram monitor inspects raw digitized frames immediately after DMA transfer, flagging overexposure when pixel counts concentrate at maximum bit depth, or flagging lens occlusion when spatial variance collapses below an empirical noise floor. A hardware watchdog timer tracks inter-arrival times across the DMA channel, flagging transport jitter when inter-frame intervals exceed $\NominalFrameInterval + 3\TimingJitter$. This empirical diagnostic heuristic does not replace the physically derived freshness deadline. Higher in the ingestion stack, an optical flow plausibility monitor compares calculated pixel displacement vectors against the body's physical velocity envelope, rejecting observations that imply accelerations beyond the chassis's mechanical limits. In multimodal configurations, cross-sensor consistency checks compare high-rate (`{python} RollingShutterSkew.f_imu_str`) inertial measurement unit (IMU) integrations against visual odometry. If visual odometry reports that the robot is stationary while the gravity-compensated IMU integration indicates sustained $2.0\text{ m/s}^2$ linear acceleration, the monitor flags a cross-modal discrepancy once attitude, sensor bias, latency, and measurement uncertainties are reconciled.

Every runtime health monitor observes the physical world through the available transducer signals. Consequently, no single sensing channel can validate its own semantic interpretations. A camera assembly with pristine optics, optimal exposure, jitter-free transport, and sub-microsecond hardware timestamping can still present an image that causes a deep neural network to hallucinate a navigable path or fail to detect an obstacle. Because deep vision backbones map high-dimensional pixel arrays through non-linear manifolds, subtle visual anomalies (a sharp shadow across an aisle, a life-sized person printed on a cardboard display, or specular glare off shrink-wrapped freight) produce valid pixel statistics, smooth optical flow fields, and misleadingly high prediction confidence. An ingestion monitor confirms that the raw data acquisition pipeline operated within nominal engineering limits, but it cannot confirm that downstream semantic inferences correspond to physical reality. Corroborating optical detections requires independent physical sensing modalities, such as lidar or millimeter-wave radar, whose coverage, beam geometry, and failure dependencies have been rigorously characterized. Even then, a validated permission path guarantees spatial clearance only within explicit operational and timing assumptions; no perception stack can guarantee unrestricted semantic truth.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-degraded-optics
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FOG CONTRAST RANGE AND WRIST-CAMERA MOTION TRAVEL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The atmospheric-scattering and motion-blur items of
# │          the environmental-degradation subsection.
# │
# │ Goal:    Range at which dense fog drops contrast to the 0.05 threshold,
# │          and camera-center travel during one wrist-camera exposure.
# │ Show:    ln(1/0.05) / 0.05 m^-1 = 60 m; 0.5 m x 3 rad/s x 5 ms = 7.5 mm.
# │ How:     Koschmieder C = C0 exp(-beta d); dx = r omega t_exp with the
# │          registry exposure of the machine's wrist camera (Sony IMX296).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class DegradedOptics:
    """Fog contrast range and wrist-camera travel within one exposure."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    beta_fog = 0.05 / meter  # category: illustrative (dense-fog extinction coefficient)
    eps_contrast = 0.05  # category: standard (5 percent contrast threshold of meteorological optical range)
    t_exp = RM.wrist_camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (registry: IMX296 configured exposure)
    r_arm = 0.5 * meter  # category: illustrative (lever arm from rotation axis to camera)
    omega = 3.0 * radian / second  # category: illustrative (sweep angular rate)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    d_fog = (math.log(1 / eps_contrast) / beta_fog).to(meter)
    dx_blur = (r_arm * omega.to(1 / second).magnitude / second * t_exp).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(d_fog.magnitude - 59.9) < 0.1, f"Unexpected fog range: {d_fog}")
    check(RM.wrist_camera.shutter_type == "global", "The wrist camera is the global-shutter IMX296.")
    check(abs(t_exp.magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected wrist exposure: {t_exp}")
    check(abs(dx_blur.magnitude - 7.5) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected blur travel: {dx_blur}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    beta_fog_str = fmt(beta_fog.to(1 / meter).magnitude, precision=2)
    eps_contrast_str = fmt(eps_contrast, precision=2)
    d_fog_str = fmt_length(round(d_fog.magnitude) * meter, unit=meter, precision=0)  # 59.9 m shown to the meter
    t_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_exp, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    r_arm_str = fmt_length(r_arm, unit=meter, precision=1)
    omega_str = fmt(omega.to(radian / second).magnitude, precision=0)
    dx_blur_str = fmt_length(dx_blur, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

### Environmental degradation under precipitation, fog, and lens flare

Physical environments continuously degrade sensory transmission across optical, near-infrared, and radio channels. A perception architecture operating across factory yards, loading docks, or public roadways must anticipate how weather and illumination alter signal-to-noise ratios without asserting hardware error flags. The running machine meets these effects at the loading dock, where daylight floods in through open bay doors and standing water collects on polished concrete; fog and rain matter for the outdoor platforms that carry the same sensors.

Optical cameras undergo severe degradation in the presence of atmospheric scattering and glare. Suspended airborne aerosol particles in fog, mist, and smoke ($1\text{ to }10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{m}$ diameter) scatter visible wavelengths ($\RadiationWavelength \approx 400\text{ to }700\text{ nm}$) under Mie scattering physics. Scene radiance attenuates exponentially across distance according to Koschmieder's law:
$$\ApparentContrast(\SightlineRange) = \ApparentContrast_0 \, e^{-\AtmosphericExtinctionCoefficient \SightlineRange}$$
where $\ApparentContrast_0$ is intrinsic object contrast, $\SightlineRange$ is metric range, and $\AtmosphericExtinctionCoefficient$ is the atmospheric extinction coefficient. In dense fog ($\AtmosphericExtinctionCoefficient \approx$ `{python} DegradedOptics.beta_fog_str` $\text{m}^{-1}$, an illustrative value), apparent contrast decays below the `{python} DegradedOptics.eps_contrast_str` perceptual detection threshold within `{python} DegradedOptics.d_fog_str`. High-frequency edge gradients dissolve into uniform background luminance, preventing convolutional and transformer backbones from forming valid feature embeddings. Airborne rain introduces high-velocity streak noise across frames, while droplets impacting the protective lens act as irregular refractive microlenses. Each droplet deflects incoming rays, creating severe localized geometric distortion, optical blur, and false object silhouettes.

Rapid angular motion compounds this degradation through motion blur and modulation transfer function (MTF) collapse.[^fn-mtf-optical-blur] During a yaw rotation or manipulator sweep, a camera center at lever arm $\SensorLeverArmLength$ travels a tangential distance set by angular rate $\AngularVelocity$ and exposure duration:
$$\FiniteChange \CameraCenterArcPosition = \SensorLeverArmLength \cdot \|\AngularVelocity\| \cdot \ExposureDuration$$
For the machine's global-shutter wrist camera at its configured `{python} DegradedOptics.t_exp_str` exposure, swept at an illustrative $\AngularSpeed =$ `{python} DegradedOptics.omega_str` rad/s on an illustrative lever arm $\SensorLeverArmLength =$ `{python} DegradedOptics.r_arm_str`, this travel scale is $\FiniteChange \CameraCenterArcPosition \approx$ `{python} DegradedOptics.dx_blur_str`. This metric displacement describes the physical travel of the optical center rather than image-plane blur in pixels. The resulting pixel displacement depends on both scene depth and focal length, while pure camera rotation shifts features across the image plane independently of depth. As motion blur smears sharp transitions across neighboring pixels, spatial gradients attenuate and feature trackers, visual odometry algorithms, and neural backbones lose tracking lock. Systems engineers must evaluate these effects across the full envelope of intended operational velocities and camera exposures.

[^fn-mtf-optical-blur]: **Modulation Transfer Function (MTF)**: The fraction of scene contrast an imaging chain passes at each spatial frequency. A uniform blur of length $\MotionBlurLength$ in the image multiplies it by a sinc that falls to zero at a period of $\MotionBlurLength$, so detail finer than the blur is erased rather than dimmed, and no network downstream can restore what the exposure removed. \index{Modulation transfer function!motion blur}

Intra-frame illumination contrast introduces another challenging failure mode through dynamic range saturation and blooming. Standard auto-exposure algorithms adjust exposure time $\ExposureDuration$ across consecutive frames to track gradual lighting changes, such as moving from a shaded warehouse aisle into an outdoor yard. However, auto-exposure cannot resolve extreme illumination differences within a single image. When a robot operating in a dim indoor aisle turns toward an open loading dock flooded with daylight, no single exposure setting suffices. An exposure long enough to resolve dark shelving units allows the intense photon flux from the dock to saturate the photodiodes, clipping those image regions to solid white. High dynamic range (HDR) sensors expand operational range by interleaving multiple exposures or employing dual-gain photodiode architectures. Yet staggered multi-exposure HDR introduces timing ambiguities that the observation contract must document: because each synthesized exposure corresponds to a distinct temporal integration window, the metadata must specify which exposure midpoint dates the frame. When extreme overexposure occurs, excess photo-generated electrons spill over potential barrier implants into neighboring pixels (**charge blooming**), washing out entire sensor columns into saturated values ($255$). Concurrently, internal reflections between lens elements generate veiling glare and lens flare streaks, eliminating the local spatial contrast essential for disparity matching and optical flow.

Active optical ranging encounters parallel limitations under degraded atmospheric conditions. Pulsed time-of-flight LiDAR, at silicon-band near-infrared wavelengths and at $1{,}550\text{ nm}$ alike, suffers three distinct physical failure mechanisms in industrial and outdoor operation:

1. *Aerosol backscatter clutter*: Emitted laser pulses strike suspended fog droplets and dust particulates, scattering optical power back into the receiver during the initial nanoseconds of time-of-flight. This creates dense near-field point clutter, often appearing as a false obstacle wall within $0.5\text{ to }3.0\text{ m}$ of the sensor aperture. Downstream spatial clustering algorithms misinterpret these backscatter returns as imminent collision hazards, triggering spurious emergency stops. Simultaneously, atmospheric extinction depletes forward pulse energy, significantly shortening maximum detection range. The magnitude of this range reduction depends on target reflectivity and the atmospheric extinction coefficient, requiring empirical calibration under the operational conditions for which the sensor is qualified.
2. *Retroreflector detector blooming and range walk*: High-visibility safety vests, barcode placards, and vehicle license plates incorporate retroreflective prismatic surfaces designed to return incident optical power directly along the emission axis at intensities orders of magnitude higher than diffuse surfaces. This massive return pulse triggers two distinct measurement errors. **Range walk**\index{LiDAR!range walk} is a temporal distortion in the receiver's avalanche photodiodes (APDs) or single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs): because a simple leading-edge discriminator triggers when an analog pulse crosses a fixed voltage threshold, a fast-rising, high-amplitude pulse trips the comparator earlier than a weak return, systematically underestimating distance to the retroreflector. While intensity-based compensation curves can correct this offset under linear amplification, they fail once the analog front-end saturates. Concurrently, **blooming** creates a spatial distortion: optical scattering and electrical crosstalk within the detector array register false returns across adjacent detector channels, surrounding the retroreflector with a spherical halo of phantom points. Sensor manufacturers reflect these physical realities in their specifications; for example, the Ouster OS1 datasheet establishes distinct, wider accuracy tolerances for retroreflective targets compared to diffuse Lambertian surfaces [@ouster2025os1].
3. *Specular surfaces and non-Lambertian forward bounce*: Triangulation systems, structured-light projectors, and time-of-flight LiDAR all assume that surfaces exhibit diffuse Lambertian scattering, reflecting incident light uniformly across the hemisphere. Specular surfaces such as polished concrete floors, shrink-wrapped freight, painted metal panels, and architectural glass violate this assumption. Emitted laser beams undergo specular mirror reflection, bouncing away from the surface normal at an angle equal to the incidence angle ($\ReflectionAngle = \IncidenceAngle$) and directing optical energy away from the receiver. On wet or polished floors, this specular bounce results in complete signal loss, creating artificial zero-return dropouts ("puddle black holes"). Against glass walls or metal structures, multi-bounce reflections cause emitted pulses to travel indirect paths back to the receiver, generating phantom point clusters that appear meters behind physical walls or deep beneath the concrete floor.

Millimeter-wave radar provides complementary all-weather capability that overcomes many optical failure modes. Operating at $76\text{ to }81\text{ GHz}$, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar uses a carrier wavelength of $\RadiationWavelength \approx 3.9\text{ mm}$, roughly 4,000 times longer than near-infrared laser light and several orders of magnitude larger than fog droplets ($1\text{ to }10\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{m}$). Scattering by such small airborne particles falls within the Rayleigh scattering regime, where the particle scattering cross-section $\ScatteringCrossSection$ scales inversely with the fourth power of wavelength:
$$\ScatteringCrossSection \propto \frac{\DropletDiameter^6}{\RadiationWavelength^4}$$
Although this extreme wavelength dependence shields radar from the severe attenuation and backscatter that paralyze optical sensors in fog and dust, radar is not immune to environmental interference. Ground reflections produce multipath ghost detections, standing water films on the radome attenuate radio-frequency signals, and low spatial resolution complicates boundary discrimination. A multimodal perception suite must therefore explicitly qualify radar coverage boundaries when primary optical streams degrade.

### Out-of-distribution inputs at the sensor boundary

Even when a sensor is calibrated, unoccluded, and operating without transport faults, its observations can fall outside the operational distribution on which downstream models were qualified. Uncertainty in these observations stems from two distinct sources. **Aleatoric uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!aleatoric} represents the irreducible physical noise of the transduction process itself, such as photon shot noise, thermal amplifier noise, or aerosol backscatter. The measurement's covariance model must quantify this uncertainty. In contrast, **epistemic uncertainty**\index{Uncertainty!epistemic} stems from the model's lack of knowledge about scenarios omitted from its training distribution, such as an overturned forklift, an unfamiliar emergency strobe pattern, or a dense chemical vapor plume. Upgrading sensor fidelity cannot eliminate epistemic uncertainty. The limits of normalized softmax scores, calibrated uncertainty estimation, and the conversion of calibrated prediction sets into action refusals lie beyond perception's scope. Perception carries a specific, narrower engineering responsibility: it must assess at the ingestion boundary whether an incoming observation appears outside the validated input support, and log that assessment directly in the observation contract.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The limits of softmax confidence and the conformal calibration that bounds it are established in @sec-brain-softmax-illusion.
:::

Input-support monitors evaluate incoming sensor frames, or early feature embeddings from the backbone, against the support of the qualification dataset. Common implementations include computing a free-energy score over unnormalized logits [@liu2020energy], measuring the Mahalanobis distance to class-conditional feature centroids [@lee2018simple], or tracking the reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained strictly on nominal operational data. Each method requires an empirical acceptance threshold calibrated against expected anomalies. An in-bounds score means only that the monitor did not flag the input under its calibrated threshold; it guarantees neither membership in the qualification distribution nor physically accurate semantic inference.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The input-support monitor these checks instantiate is established in @sec-evaluation-limits.
:::

When an input-support monitor detects an anomaly, the perception pipeline sets a `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` flag in the health bitmask that every observation carries, one of the record fields that @sec-perception-observation-contract assembles. The permission path monitors this bitmask to disallow high-speed motions, expand conservative clearance buffers, or trigger a deterministic supervisory fallback. In multimodal systems, the same bitmask arbitrates between sensors. On the running machine, if the navigation camera raises `BIT_OPTICAL_SATURATED` or `BIT_OOD_DETECTED` while the LiDAR's returns stay healthy, the pipeline demotes the camera's tokens and the rack-end claim rests on LiDAR range alone, provided the LiDAR is independently validated to enforce spatial clearance under those operating conditions. Outdoor platforms apply the same arbitration with radar in the LiDAR's place.

::: {#ws-perception-tesla-williston-omission .callout-war-story title="Silent perception omission (2016)"}
**Context**: A 2015 Tesla Model S\index{Incidents!Williston accident} traveling at about $74\text{ mph}$ with Traffic-Aware Cruise Control and Autosteer active struck a refrigerated semitrailer turning left across its path near Williston, Florida [@ntsb2017tesla].

**Mechanism**: The crossing-path collision lay outside the front-to-rear crash modes for which the 2015 warning and automatic braking systems were designed. NHTSA reported that automatic braking required agreement between camera and radar; unusual vehicle shapes could impede camera classification ([NHTSA ODI PE16-007](https://static.nhtsa.gov/odi/inv/2016/INCLA-PE16007-7876.PDF)).

**Impact**: The NTSB found no recorded indication that forward collision warning or automatic emergency braking detected an object, and no pre-impact braking occurred. The vehicle passed beneath the turning semitrailer, shearing off the car's roof; the paired investigation photographs in @fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash document this physical outcome, highlighting collision scrape damage along the right underside of the trailer alongside the roofless passenger cabin.

**Response**: The NTSB examined operational design domain limits and driver engagement as well as the collision-avoidance systems.

**Systems lesson**: An absent detection is not evidence that a crossing path is clear. A permission design must account for detection coverage and unsupported scenarios; a health flag cannot certify that every relevant object was perceived.
:::

::: {#fig-08-real-ntsb-williston-crash fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Williston collision damage**: This NTSB presentation slide shows damage on the right side of the semitrailer and the roofless Tesla after the 2016 crash. The crossing-path geometry and absence of pre-impact braking come from the [NTSB accident report](https://www.ntsb.gov/investigations/AccidentReports/Reports/HAR1702.pdf), not from the photographs alone. (Source: NTSB board-meeting presentation for report HAR-17/02; photographs courtesy of Florida Highway Patrol)." fig-alt="NTSB slide with two photographs: left, a refrigerated semitrailer with damage low on its right side; right, a heavily damaged roofless Tesla. Yellow ovals mark damage areas. The photos do not show the vehicles' motion or collision angle."}
![](images/png/fig08_real_ntsb_williston_crash.png){width="90%"}
:::

An observation contract can expose only the physical, temporal, and distributional faults that the ingestion layer is designed to measure. Detectable interface errors, transport jitter, and out-of-distribution feature shifts are readily encoded into explicit health bitmasks. Silent semantic omissions, such as the missed detection at Williston, evade single-sensor health checks. Preventing catastrophic failures requires an architectural safety design: incorporating independent physical sensing modalities, enforcing conservative spatial permission envelopes, and never mistaking the absence of an error flag for confirmation of physical safety. Omission can also depend on who is in view: a detector qualified mostly on people standing upright can miss a kneeling worker or a child more often, so any detection rate a contract reports for people holds only for the groups it was measured on.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How a detection gap between groups of people becomes a gap in stopping distance and impact energy, and how large each group's sample must be, is developed in @sec-responsibility-perception-disparity.
:::

## The Observation Contract {#sec-perception-observation-contract}

A downstream tracker, policy backbone, or permission path cannot reconstruct exposure timing, mounting calibration, or byte integrity from a raw tensor alone. The perception subsystem therefore wraps each sensory output in an **observation contract**\index{Observation contract!definition}\index{Perception!observation contract}, the sixth record in the book's sixteen-record chain. In closed-loop physical systems, an observation is unusable without an explicit capture epoch, an identified clock domain, a bounded conversion to the permission path's clock, and an extrinsic calibration operating within its qualified validity envelope. A safe consumer must reject any incoming record lacking these guarantees before inspecting a single payload byte. The system's shared clock domain and $\SignalHandoff_1$ age budget originate in the nervous-system handoff record of @sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix; perception, in turn, provides the capture-side timestamps and uncertainty bounds that downstream consumers need to verify compliance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The sixteen-record chain, in which the observation contract is Record 6, is developed in @sec-appendix-systems-record-register.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-handoff-sensor-age
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SENSOR-SIDE AGE AGAINST THE H_1 HANDOFF ALLOTMENT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The handoff paragraph of @sec-perception-observation-contract.
# │
# │ Goal:    Reconcile the handoff matrix's sensor-age allotment (one frame
# │          period) with this chapter's exposure-midpoint-plus-readout age.
# │ Show:    16.7 ms frame period; 24.6 ms from the top row's exposure midpoint
# │          to the end of readout; 16.3 ms from the middle row's; the top-row
# │          convention exceeds the allotment by 7.9 ms.
# │ How:     RM.nav_camera frame rate, exposure, and readout. The allotment is
# │          taken as one frame period, matching the handoff matrix value.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class HandoffSensorAge:
    """Sensor-side age of the navigation camera under two row conventions."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: navigation camera)
    t_exp = camera.exposure_time.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (configured exposure)
    t_readout = camera.readout_time.to(millisecond)  # category: datasheet
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_frame = (1 / f_frame).to(millisecond)
    age_top = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout).to(millisecond)
    age_mid = (t_exp / 2 + t_readout / 2).to(millisecond)
    excess_top = (age_top - t_frame).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_frame.magnitude - 16.7) < 0.05, f"Unexpected frame period: {t_frame}")
    check(abs(age_top.magnitude - 24.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected top-row sensor age: {age_top}")
    check(abs(age_mid.magnitude - 16.3) < 0.05, f"Unexpected middle-row sensor age: {age_mid}")
    check(age_mid < t_frame < age_top, "Prose says only the middle-row convention fits the allotment")
    check(abs(excess_top.magnitude - 7.9) < 0.05, f"Unexpected excess: {excess_top}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    age_top_str = fmt_latency(age_top, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    age_mid_str = fmt_latency(age_mid, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    excess_top_str = fmt_latency(excess_top, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

Formally, the contract couples either a raw observation tensor or an extracted geometric bounding envelope with the validation metadata that downstream consumers require (@eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple):
$$\mathcal{O} = \langle \CaptureTimestamp, \text{clock\_id}, \ClockConversionBound, \text{frame\_id}, \ObservationPayload, \BodyFramePointCovariance, \ClearanceInset, \text{mask}_{\text{health}}, \text{crc32} \rangle$$ {#eq-percep-observation-contract-tuple}
In this tuple, $\CaptureTimestamp$ records the exposure-midpoint timestamp registered on monotonic clock $\text{clock\_id}$, $\ClockConversionBound$ bounds the maximum synchronization error when converting to the clock of the safety MCU that hosts the permission path, and $\text{frame\_id}$ identifies the calibrated sensor transform. The payload $\ObservationPayload$ contains the raw sensor array or derived geometric bounding envelope, $\BodyFramePointCovariance$ characterizes its spatial covariance, $\ClearanceInset$ provides the qualified clearance inset, $\text{mask}_{\text{health}}$ conveys hardware and perceptual health status bits, and $\text{crc32}$ seals both header and payload against transport corruption. Spatial memory consumes this record to update its world model, while trajectory planning uses $\ClearanceInset$ to inflate collision boundaries; both modules evaluate evidence age, verify kinematic coordinate frames, and bound spatial uncertainty before allowing an observation to influence a control decision.

The tuple is the same object as the error-qualified claim $(\BodyFramePoint, \BodyFramePointCovariance, \ClearanceInset, \DispatchObservationAge)$ that @sec-perception-error-clearance assembled, now wrapped for transport. The claim's point travels in $\ObservationPayload$, its covariance in $\BodyFramePointCovariance$, and its inset in $\ClearanceInset$. Its age is deliberately not stored, because each consumer computes the current evidence age from $\CaptureTimestamp$ and $\ClockConversionBound$ on its own clock.

This contract does not replace binary serialization formats such as Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, or ROS 2 IDL. In fact, any of these serialization systems can transmit the underlying struct over shared memory or bus fabrics. While transport schemas standardize memory layout and data types, the observation contract establishes verifiable physical invariants: monotonic temporal progression, bounded clock skew, active calibration validity windows, and rigorous spatial uncertainty limits. @Tbl-08-observation-record-schema serializes the tuple as named fields, details each one alongside its validation rule, and populates the schema for the mobile manipulator's navigation camera. It splits $\CaptureTimestamp$ and $\text{clock\_id}$ into `capture_timestamp_ns` and `capture_clock_id`, carries the calibration behind $\text{frame\_id}$ in `calibration_metadata`, and adds a `sequence_index` and a `provenance_digest` that the tuple leaves out.

```{python}
#| label: calc-perception-nav-observation-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NAVIGATION-CAMERA OBSERVATION RECORD, FILLED
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The filled column of @tbl-08-observation-record-schema and the
# │          clock-conversion paragraph that follows it.
# │
# │ Goal:    Fill the observation record for the mobile manipulator's
# │          navigation camera and size the consumer's upper age at dispatch.
# │ Show:    age at dispatch 51.6 ms; clock-conversion bound 0.2 ms; upper
# │          age 51.8 ms, equal to the refusal threshold (budgeted age plus
# │          bound); frame counter at 60 Hz; the bound's 0.3 mm of travel at
# │          the 1.5 m/s drive limit, carried inside delta_loc rather than
# │          charged as a budget row.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age (the latency waterfall above); eps_sync is a
# │          chapter LOAD value that the spatial-belief record of @sec-memory
# │          reuses; RM.nav_camera frame rate; displacement via
# │          calc_spatial_information_age_displacement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_length, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class NavObservationRecord:
    """Filled observation record for the running machine's navigation camera."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    camera = RM.nav_camera  # category: datasheet (registry: Sony IMX477 navigation camera)
    f_frame = camera.frame_rate  # category: datasheet
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age.to(millisecond)  # category: derived
    eps_sync = 0.2 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (capture-to-MCU clock-conversion bound; reused by @sec-memory)
    v = RM.base.max_velocity.to(meter / second)  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    upper_age = (t_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)
    refuse_threshold = (AISLE.perception_age + eps_sync).to(millisecond)  # refusal threshold: budgeted age plus the conversion bound
    dx_sync = calc_spatial_information_age_displacement(v, eps_sync).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_age.magnitude - 51.6) < 0.05, f"Unexpected age at dispatch: {t_age}")
    check(abs(eps_sync.to(millisecond).magnitude - 0.2) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected clock-conversion bound: {eps_sync}")
    check(abs(upper_age.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected upper age at dispatch: {upper_age}")
    check(abs(refuse_threshold.magnitude - 51.8) < 0.05, f"Unexpected refusal threshold: {refuse_threshold}")
    check(abs((refuse_threshold - upper_age).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Prose says the dispatched upper age meets the refusal threshold exactly")
    check(abs(f_frame.to(hertz).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected navigation-camera frame rate: {f_frame}")
    check(abs(dx_sync.magnitude - 0.3) < 0.005, f"Unexpected travel during the clock-conversion bound: {dx_sync}")
    check(dx_sync < delta_loc, "Prose says the clock-conversion travel fits inside delta_loc")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    eps_sync_str = fmt_latency(eps_sync.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    upper_age_str = fmt_latency(upper_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    refuse_threshold_str = fmt_latency(refuse_threshold, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_frame_str = fmt_frequency(f_frame, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    dx_sync_str = fmt_length(dx_sync, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

| Record field                               | Meaning                                                                                                                 | Consumer check                                                                                     | Navigation camera                                                                                                                                                           |
|:-------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `capture_timestamp_ns`, `capture_clock_id` | Exposure midpoint in one shared, monotonic capture clock                                                                | Convert to safety microcontroller (MCU) time with a valid bounded-skew mapping before checking age | Trigger edge plus $\ExposureDuration/2$ (top-row exposure midpoint) on clock `cam_nav`; dispatched `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` later (@tbl-08-latency-budget) |
| `sync_error_ns`                            | Bound on capture-to-MCU clock conversion error                                                                          | Add to worst-case age; refuse if missing or expired                                                | `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str`, so the upper age at dispatch is `{python} NavObservationRecord.upper_age_str`                                                 |
| `sequence_index`                           | Monotonic camera frame counter                                                                                          | Detect gaps and reordering                                                                         | One count per frame at `{python} NavObservationRecord.f_frame_str`                                                                                                          |
| `sensor_frame_id`                          | Transform-tree key and calibration revision                                                                             | Select the valid extrinsic transform                                                               | `nav_cam` with its calibration revision                                                                                                                                     |
| `tensor_payload`                           | Format, dimensions, length, and buffer                                                                                  | Validate bounds and record checksum before reading                                                 | Raw/debayered image tensor or point-cloud buffer                                                                                                                            |
| `bounding_envelope`                        | Bounding volume $[d\CartesianXCoordinate, d\CartesianYCoordinate, d\CartesianZCoordinate]$ or qualified clearance inset | Bound occupied volume and inflate safety sets ($\ClearanceInset$)                                  | Metric corridor bounds inflated by validated quantile                                                                                                                       |
| `spatial_covariance`                       | Positive-semidefinite spatial error scale                                                                               | Use with separately calibrated bias and tail bounds                                                | Point-wise or object-centric covariance matrix $\BodyFramePointCovariance$                                                                                                  |
| `calibration_metadata`                     | Intrinsics, extrinsics, coefficients, temperature, validity range                                                       | Reject calibration outside its validated region                                                    | Factory pinhole $\CameraIntrinsicCalibrationMatrix$ and chassis extrinsic transform $\CameraExtrinsicTransform$                                                             |
| `provenance_digest`                        | SHA-256 of firmware and model revisions                                                                                 | Match the approved build; this is not payload integrity                                            | Signed hash of vision backbone weights and firmware                                                                                                                         |
| `payload_crc32`                            | CRC over serialized header (excluding this field) and payload                                                           | Detect accidental record corruption; not authentication                                            | 32-bit cyclical redundancy check                                                                                                                                            |
| `health_bitmask`                           | Hardware, degradation, and perception validity flags                                                                    | Refuse claims with safety-critical faults or OOD flags                                             | Sync-loss, link, saturation, rain/fog clutter, and OOD bits; input-support bits                                                                                             |

: **Observation contract schema**: Compact fields needed to date and frame a claim, evaluate its uncertainty, bounding envelope, and health flags, and check the bytes and generating revision. The last column fills the fields this chapter computes for the mobile manipulator's navigation camera; its dispatch age and clock-conversion bound are illustrative. A keyed authenticator is a separate requirement if the threat model includes malicious modification. {#tbl-08-observation-record-schema tbl-colwidths="[23,23,26,28]"}

The fields detailed in @tbl-08-observation-record-schema anchor each observation in physical time, geometric space, and software revision history. The capture timestamp $\CaptureTimestamp$ must refer to a strictly monotonic hardware timer rather than wall-clock time (such as nanoseconds since the UNIX epoch), which remains vulnerable to stepping backward during network time adjustments. Because rolling-shutter sensors read out scan lines sequentially, any spatial claim derived from a rolling-shutter imager must explicitly identify the image row or region corresponding to that capture instant. The transport-level `sequence_index` counter detects frame drops and out-of-order deliveries directly on the bus, independently of clock readings. When the safety MCU operates in a separate clock domain from the camera host, an active synchronization daemon provides a versioned affine mapping $\MicrocontrollerClockTime = \ClockConversionSlope \CaptureTimestamp + \ClockConversionIntercept$, an expiration window, and an empirical sync-error bound $\ClockConversionBound$, characterized as described in @sec-perception-qualifying-error.

Systems engineering demands precise conventions when accounting for sensor latency. The handoff matrix and the perception latency budget evaluate the sensor's latency contribution under different row conventions, and the observation contract must explicitly state which convention governs the record. The handoff matrix allots $\SignalHandoff_1$ one frame period (`{python} HandoffSensorAge.t_frame_str` at `{python} HandoffSensorAge.f_frame_str`) and references the entire frame by its middle row. Measuring from that middle row's exposure midpoint to the completion of sensor readout yields a sensor-side latency of $\ExposureDuration/2 + \SensorReadoutTime/2 =$ `{python} HandoffSensorAge.age_mid_str`, which falls well within the handoff allotment. Conversely, the perception latency waterfall charges for the top row: $\ExposureDuration/2 + \SensorReadoutTime =$ `{python} HandoffSensorAge.age_top_str`. Because a physical hazard such as a warehouse rack upright can appear in the very first scan lines, a safety-certified stopping budget must charge for the oldest sensory evidence underpinning the spatial claim. Under this oldest-row convention, the navigation camera exceeds the handoff allotment by `{python} HandoffSensorAge.excess_top_str`. The two numbers answer different questions, and the stopping budget governs. The $\SignalHandoff_1$ allotment is a design budget for the sensing handoff, stated in the middle-row convention, and the camera meets it. The safety charge is row five, which uses this chapter's oldest-row waterfall. The `{python} HandoffSensorAge.excess_top_str` is already inside the `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` that row five charges, so nothing is missing from the stopping budget. What the mismatch does require is a record that says which convention dated it. The capture metadata therefore stamps the reference row index, so that a consumer checking $\SignalHandoff_1$ and a consumer checking clearance each read the age they need from the same field.

Upon dispatching an observation, the producer records an upper bound on its observation age at dispatch as $\McuDispatchTime - \McuCaptureTime + \ClockConversionBound$. That metric reflects only the latency accumulated up to the producer's egress boundary. By the time the permission path admits the record, the evidence has aged further by the dispatch-to-admission transit delay $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$, and it ages further still before actuators execute a command. The permission path must evaluate freshness using its local monotonic clock against the original capture epoch; treating a static dispatch timestamp as if time had frozen violates basic physical causality. Submitting a new trajectory proposal derived from a previously buffered observation does not refresh the underlying sensory evidence.

For the navigation camera, the **dispatch-local** threshold equals the budgeted observation age `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` plus the `{python} NavObservationRecord.eps_sync_str` clock-conversion bound, yielding `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str`. The threshold sits exactly at the budget because row five of the stopping budget charges exactly that age; admitting an older frame would spend travel that no row accounts for. A frame that meets every stage budget therefore reaches dispatch with zero spare margin, and any host contention, pipeline queuing, or batching beyond those budgets pushes it past the threshold. The stage values are allocations each stage must meet at its tail, not typical latencies, so a pipeline that meets them refuses only the frames that overrun them. In the vehicle's stopping budget, the `{python} NavObservationRecord.t_age_str` perception delay maps directly to physical travel distance at cruising velocity, while the `{python} NavObservationRecord.dx_sync_str` displacement associated with the clock-conversion uncertainty bound is absorbed into the localization uncertainty parameter $\LocalizationBound$. Neither accounting choice eliminates the ongoing physical aging that occurs after dispatch.

Admitting an observation into the motion-planning safety pipeline requires an empirically qualified current-age limit that accounts for the dispatch-to-admission bound $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ while reserving sufficient execution time for the active motion lease and physical braking response. Because this partial budget has not yet bounded $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$, the populated record in @tbl-08-observation-record-schema illustrates correct structural field construction rather than an admitted full-speed trajectory. Once engineers measure and bound $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ across all inter-process channels, they can either close the stopping budget or reduce maximum vehicle velocity to restore safety margins. Systems latency accounting requires strict conservation of time: whether an engineer anchors the timeline at physical capture or measures from the admission gate by summing prior evidence age with the active lease, each elapsed interval appears exactly once in the stopping budget.

The transform identifier `sensor_frame_id` and its calibration revision key the observation into the robot's kinematic transform tree.[^fn-stereo-baseline-thermal] The provenance digest records the exact SHA-256 hash of the vision model weights and camera firmware, providing an auditable record of software configuration. Concurrently, `payload_crc32` guards against transmission glitches across shared-memory rings or serial buses. Systems designers must distinguish data integrity from semantic truth: checksums and build digests detect accidental bit flips and firmware mismatches, but they cannot verify whether an image is optically uncorrupted, nor do they prevent adversarial tampering without a keyed cryptographic signature.

[^fn-stereo-baseline-thermal]: **Stereo Baseline Thermal Drift**\index{Hardware!thermal expansion}: For a stereo baseline $\StereoBaseline =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.b_str` and an unmodeled change $|\SmallPerturbation \StereoBaseline| =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.db_str`, first-order geometry gives $|\SmallPerturbation \CameraFrameDepth|/\CameraFrameDepth\approx|\SmallPerturbation \StereoBaseline|/\StereoBaseline$. At $\CameraFrameDepth =$ `{python} StereoDepthError.z_thermal_str`, the corresponding depth bias is about `{python} StereoDepthError.dz_thermal_str`, assuming focal length and disparity are otherwise unchanged. Temperature compensation must be checked against the actual mount and calibration.

The `health_bitmask` structures failure reporting across three architectural layers. The lowest bits report hardware-level faults, such as clock synchronization loss, DMA ring buffer overruns, or physical link dropouts. The intermediate bits signal environmental degradation, including sensor saturation from direct sunlight, optical blooming, and aerosol backscatter from dust or fog. The upper bits represent perceptual validity concerns, such as severe field-of-view occlusion or out-of-distribution (OOD) sensory inputs that fall outside the training support tested during system evaluation. When any safety-critical bit is set, downstream motion planners and trackers must immediately reject spatial claims derived from that frame.

An explicit observation schema also creates a systematic interface for automated fault injection. Verification harnesses can deterministically alter capture timestamps, drop sequence numbers, artificially inflate covariance diagonals, or assert occlusion bits, confirming that downstream consumers reject or gracefully degrade unviable observations within their budgeted time limits. These software mutations demonstrate consumer responses for the tested corruptions under the tested budgets; evaluating resilience against physical phenomena such as optical flare, mounting deflection, and actuator dynamics requires hardware-in-the-loop testing regimes.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Hardware-in-the-loop testing of physical phenomena is operationalized in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

Learned policies require explicit contract metadata just as much as classical state estimators do. An end-to-end policy $\CognitivePolicyAction_{t} = \pi(\CapturedSensorObservation)$ that receives only sensory pixels or point clouds cannot distinguish two identical images consumed under radically different pipeline latencies. Widely used vision-language-action (VLA) models do not receive these quantities. RT-2 and OpenVLA condition on visual tokens and a language prompt [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla], and $\pi_0$ adds proprioceptive joint state [@black2024pi0], but none of them is given capture age, extrinsic transforms, or measurement covariance as input. To integrate learned models safely into real-time control loops, this book presents an **observation tokenizer** that projects the full observation contract into the token space of a VLA policy or neural estimator. The sensory modality dictates the raw payload encoding (patch tokens from vision transformers, range tokens from lidar arrays, spike tokens from event cameras, or stress fields from tactile arrays), while the tokenizer interface preserves the capture epoch, geometric frame, and measurement uncertainty associated with that payload.

Under this architecture, the observation tokenizer pairs the sensory feature tokens $\SensorFeatureTokens$ with continuous Fourier temporal embeddings ($\CaptureAgeEmbedding = \text{Fourier}(\CurrentWallClockTime - \TimeInstant_0)$), coordinate frame prefix embeddings ($\CoordinateFrameEmbedding = \text{MLP}(\CameraExtrinsicTransform)$), and spatial covariance embeddings ($\SpatialCovarianceEmbedding = \text{MLP}(\text{vec}(\BodyFramePointCovariance))$) (@eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer):
$$\ObservationTokenSequence = [\SensorFeatureTokens, \CaptureAgeEmbedding, \CoordinateFrameEmbedding, \SpatialCovarianceEmbedding]$$ {#eq-percep-vla-obs-tokenizer}
A forward-propagated state token $\PredictedStateEmbedding = \text{MLP}(\CurrentStateEstimate)$, generated by the state estimator that spatial memory maintains, can accompany these tokens so the policy conditions on the robot's predicted state at the instant of actuation rather than its historical configuration at sensor exposure. While this embedding scheme exposes physical time, frame geometry, and uncertainty directly to transformer attention layers, engineers must verify that the model actually attends to these tokens in closed-loop operation. Demonstrating that a policy uses temporal embeddings requires rigorous ablation experiments that inject artificial latency into held-out evaluation trials and measure resulting closed-loop tracking error. Furthermore, embedding metadata as neural tokens does not substitute for deterministic safety gating: the permission path must continue to verify clock bounds, extrinsic calibration envelopes, innovation residuals, and health status bits before any network output is permitted to drive the physical actuators.

::: {#chk-percep-observation-contract-triage .callout-checkpoint title="Observation contract checks"}

A consumer can refuse only what the record lets it check, and it must check before it reads the payload.

- [ ] **Record triage**: Can you explain why a health bit, checksum, valid clock conversion, and freshness check must precede consumption of a spatial claim?
- [ ] **Timestamp corruption vs. dropped packets**: Can you describe why receiving a sensory frame with a desynchronized timestamp degrades spatial state estimation and policy grounding far more severely than dropping the packet entirely?
- [ ] **Deterministic fault injection**: Can you distinguish between physically perturbing optical sensors vs. deterministically mutating fields in the shared-memory observation contract during automated hardware-in-the-loop verification?
- [ ] **Age on the consumer's clock**: Can you explain why the permission path must recompute evidence age on its own monotonic clock from the capture epoch, rather than trusting the age stamped at dispatch, and why its `{python} NavObservationRecord.refuse_threshold_str` dispatch-local threshold is not the limit it applies at admission?

:::

Because the observation contract preserves the exact capture epoch, delayed frames do not become worthless garbage. When network congestion or compute preemption delays delivery, a state estimator can ingest an out-of-order observation at the precise historical instant it captured and propagate corrections forward to the current state, a technique that spatial memory develops in @sec-perception-discrete-state-estimation. Nevertheless, successfully passing contract triage and computing state updates does not make an observation semantically true in the physical world. The following common pitfalls illustrate how systems engineers confuse syntactically validated records with genuine physical reality.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-perception-fallacies-pitfalls}

Perception\index{Perception} must describe the physical world within the strict temporal deadlines demanded by closed-loop control. In embodied systems, high semantic confidence and fine spatial resolution cannot compensate for pipelines that deliver stale observations, fuse asynchronous exposures, or treat average I/O bandwidth as a bound on single-frame latency.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Accepting an observation because its semantic classification confidence is high, regardless of its age.*

Consider a mobile manipulator that receives an observation indicating with high semantic confidence that the rack end ahead is clear. If a scheduling stall in the vision pipeline\index{Perception!pipeline latency} delivers that observation several frames late, a warehouse worker who stepped into the aisle after the camera exposure will not appear in the image. The confidence score\index{Confidence score} describes only the classifier's assessment of past sensory input, not current physical clearance. Treating an overdue packet as present state risks commanding actuators directly into occupied space. The perception interface must verify measurement age against its freshness limit (@sec-perception-observation-contract)\index{Observation!freshness limit} and reject observations that exceed the threshold. Furthermore, any state propagation\index{State estimation!propagation} that continues without fresh data must inflate kinematic uncertainty covariances\index{Kinematics!uncertainty}, incorporating heavy-tailed residuals or reachability bounds on dynamic obstacles. This growth forces downstream controllers to contract their safety envelopes\index{Safety!envelope} and slow the robot as sensory evidence ages. High softmax confidence reflects internal model certainty on an acquired image, but it guarantees neither temporal freshness nor true physical clearance.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Fusing multi-sensor observations without a clock bound derived from the tolerated spatial error.*

Suppose two cameras on the mobile manipulator observe the same rack upright while the mobile base travels at its `{python} RackEndOpeningAge.v_str` velocity limit, but their internal clocks differ by an uncorrected skew $\InterSensorClockSkew$. If downstream fusion treats the two exposure times\index{Exposure time} as simultaneous, the physical upright appears displaced by $\BodySpeed\,\InterSensorClockSkew$ between the two sensor frames. Downstream track association\index{Track association} can split this single physical obstacle into two conflicting tracks ("ghosting"), corrupting the world model. Spatial calibration\index{Calibration!spatial} cannot correct an uncharacterized temporal offset. Instead, the allowable clock synchronization error must follow directly from the tolerated spatial position error $\ToleratedPositionError$ and the maximum operational velocity $\SpeedBound$, yielding the relation $\InterSensorClockSkew \le \ToleratedPositionError / \SpeedBound$. Hardware synchronization\index{Hardware!clock synchronization} at exposure time makes that bound enforceable. Selecting a network timing technology such as the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP)\index{IEEE 1588 PTP} without first deriving this spatial error budget leaves the sensor fusion pipeline ungrounded.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Inferring a critical read's deadline from average camera bandwidth.*

A comfortable average utilization figure says nothing about how long a critical read stalls behind synchronized sensor capture and inference bursts. On the mobile manipulator, safety permission checks execute on a dedicated real-time microcontroller reading from local memory, shielding the immediate control path from host bus contention. The danger instead appears on the application processor: concurrent DMA transfers, memory bus saturation, and inference bursts delay the sensor ingestion pipeline (@sec-perception-cost-ingestion). This contention inflates the capture-to-dispatch age of the perceptual observation and stretches the renewal interval between successive updates. System architects must verify worst-case capture-to-dispatch age and end-to-end renewal intervals under peak burst conditions rather than relying on average throughput metrics.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming an end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy implicitly learns to compensate for rolling shutter and sensor latency without explicit temporal tokenization.*

Deep imitation learning often assumes that large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained on extensive robot teleoperation datasets will automatically learn action corrections that compensate for sensor distortion and communication latency. In practice, demonstration datasets aggregate trajectories collected across fluctuating chassis velocities, camera frame rates, and host bus loads. If the model receives only raw pixel arrays without capture timestamps or row readout schedules, it cannot distinguish true physical obstacle geometry from rolling-shutter scanline shear or motion lag. Unresolved temporal ambiguity degrades closed-loop trajectory tracking and induces control oscillations. The quadratic compounding bound of @eq-data-quadratic-drift describes how per-step imitation error grows over a horizon, but it assumes a stationary Markov process rather than unmodeled phase lags and sensor dynamics. Providing explicit timing metadata, such as capture time deltas ($\FiniteChange \TimeInstant = \CurrentWallClockTime - \TimeInstant_0$), readout offsets, and forward-propagated kinematic states, gives the network the causal context required to resolve these distortions. Even with temporal tokenization, empirical evaluation must verify closed-loop stability, and independent out-of-band safety permission checks remain mandatory.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating neural depth network outputs as calibrated geometric covariances without empirical residual validation.*

Monocular depth estimation backbones and bird's-eye-view (BEV) lifting transformers output continuous depth fields or discrete depth-bin categorical distributions. Engineers often mistake these softmax spreads or secondary network confidence heads for calibrated geometric uncertainties ($\BodyFramePointCovariance$), passing them directly into extended Kalman filters or control barrier functions. In practice, raw neural confidence scores correlate poorly with true physical error distributions. When presented with unfamiliar textures, specular reflections, or occluding object silhouettes, depth networks produce gross multimodal outliers that deviate by tens of standard deviations from physical ground truth. Downstream clearance insets ($\ClearanceInset$) must never rely on raw neural variance. Safe execution requires empirical validation against heavy-tailed residual distributions and hard spatial bounds cross-verified by active ranging sensors such as LiDAR or radar.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying exclusively on line-of-sight optical sensing for manipulation without tactile contact feedback.*

During reaches and grasps, the robot's own fingers, palm, and wrist occlude the contact interface. Optical cameras cannot observe local normal forces, shear stress distributions, or incipient micro-slip at the boundary between the gripper and the object. Relying exclusively on high-resolution visual perception to ensure grasp stability leads to dropped objects from undetected slipping or crushed workpieces from excessive actuator torque. Tasks that involve physical interaction and delicate object handling require direct contact feedback. Elastomeric tactile sensors and optical skin arrays can track surface shear and incipient micro-slip, while other applications may rely on wrist force-torque transducers, compliant passive mechanics, or fixtured tooling. Sensor selection must reflect the physical contact dynamics of the manipulation task rather than defaulting to line-of-sight optical cameras.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming active LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to specular reflections and multipath interference in built environments.*

A common misconception is that active time-of-flight LiDAR and depth sensors are immune to optical artifacts because they project their own structured energy. In industrial facilities and built environments, surfaces routinely violate the diffuse Lambertian scattering assumption. Polished concrete floors, metallic shelving, architectural glass partitions, and shrink-wrapped pallet freight cause severe specular reflection. Emitted laser pulses deflect away from the receiver at shallow incidence angles, causing complete signal loss and creating artificial dropouts ("puddle black holes") on polished or wet floors. Conversely, multi-bounce reflections bounce pulses across multiple reflective surfaces before returning to the detector, generating phantom obstacles that appear meters behind solid walls or beneath the floor plane. The observation pipeline must validate return intensity distributions and cross-corroborate surface geometry against complementary inertial and radar channels.

:::

## Summary {#sec-perception-summary}

A perception measurement is actionable only when its capture epoch, clock synchronization bound, coordinate frame, and spatial uncertainty match the kinematic requirements of the intended motion. Sensor selection begins with the physical quantity demanded by the control decision: photometric appearance, metric range, Doppler radial velocity, or contact deformation. Physical capture constraints then determine the exact temporal and geometric validity of that measurement. For rolling-shutter cameras, row-by-row readout creates geometric distortion that must be compensated before triangulation, while an optical bearing ray provides directional bearing but no distance until stereo disparity or active time-of-flight ranging resolves depth. Furthermore, calibration matrices remain valid only within the physical and environmental envelopes under which they were characterized. Latency between exposure and downstream dispatch directly consumes the vehicle's stopping budget. At the drive limit, the first five rows of that budget leave `{python} SensorInformationAge.remaining_str` of the `{python} SensorInformationAge.d_clear_str` clear distance, a remainder that must still absorb the dispatch-to-admission interval, the jerk-limited stop, and the tracking inset. Whether the machine may drive at that speed is therefore a question this chapter hands forward to @sec-placement-dispatch-admission and @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes, which close the budget; @tbl-enforcement-stopping-budget lists every term with the chapter that prices it. Because an embodied system continues to travel while sensor data moves through serialization, transport, neural inference, and planner admission, unmeasured pipeline delays erode physical clearance margins just as severely as spatial measurement error.

Spatial error deducts from that same physical clearance budget. Stereo depth uncertainty scales quadratically with distance under fixed disparity noise, while angular extrinsic misalignment introduces lever-arm errors that widen linearly with range. System designers cannot rely on nominal datasheets or raw model outputs to establish safety bounds. Zero-mean covariance matrices frequently ignore systematic calibration biases, and classification confidences or learned depth logits do not represent calibrated tail probabilities. Establishing a rigorous 99th-percentile clearance inset requires empirical residual quantiles evaluated directly against ground-truth measurements across the operational domain. Perception delivers individual dated, localized, and qualified measurements; integrating these discrete observations into a coherent state estimate that remains reliable between sensor arrivals is the responsibility of spatial memory.

Silent failures present the most severe operational hazards in physical systems, precisely because dropped frames or overt hardware faults trigger immediate system alerts, whereas misdated frames, saturated detectors, or hallucinated traversable paths arrive without raising error flags. To guard against corrupted data, the perception pipeline enforces an explicit observation contract. Downstream consumers inspect and validate the capture timestamp, clock synchronization bound, reference frame, calibration identifier, error model, and hardware health flags before reading payload buffers. Even with rigorous contracts, confirming semantic truth requires corroboration across independent, complementary sensing modalities.

Seven relations carry the chapter's quantitative argument, and @tbl-08-key-equations records what each bounds or decides.

| Equation                                                                                                                                                            | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                                                       | Derived                          |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| $\ObservationAgeDisplacement = \int_{{\CaptureTimestamp}_0}^{{\CaptureTimestamp}_0+\DispatchObservationAge} \Velocity(\TimeInstant)\,d\TimeInstant$                 | The travel an observation's age costs before any consumer can react; at constant speed, $\SpeedAtDetection\,\DispatchObservationAge$ enters the stopping budget | @eq-percep-spatial-displacement  |
| $\DispatchObservationAge = \tfrac{1}{2}\ExposureDuration + \SensorReadoutTime + \dots + \PerceptionDispatchTime$                                                    | The capture-to-dispatch age of serialized stages, and which stage dominates it; overlapping stages need a measured interval instead                             | @eq-percep-latency-waterfall     |
| $\RollingShutterDistortion(\SensorRowIndex) = \Velocity\,\SensorRowIndex\,\RollingShutterRowReadout$                                                                | The along-track shear a rolling shutter records, which must be removed before the estimator spends $\LocalizationBound$ on it                                   | @eq-percep-rolling-shutter-skew  |
| $\lvert\SmallPerturbation \CameraFrameDepth\rvert \approx \dfrac{\CameraFrameDepth^2}{\FocalLength \StereoBaseline}\lvert\SmallPerturbation \StereoDisparity\rvert$ | How fast stereo depth error grows with range, and so the range beyond which one standard deviation consumes an allowance                                        | @eq-percep-stereo-uncertainty    |
| $\ClearanceInset = \RequiredClearance + \lVert\SpatialErrorVector\rVert_{\text{p99}}$                                                                               | The clearance a consumer holds so the true obstacle stays outside $\RequiredClearance$ except with the measured tail probability                                | @eq-percep-clearance-inset       |
| $\FiniteChange \CartesianPosition = \Velocity\,\SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant + \tfrac{1}{2} \LinearAcceleration\,(\SmallPerturbation \TimeInstant)^2$             | The position error a misdated observation carries silently, the reason a wrong timestamp is worse than a lost frame                                             | @eq-percep-kinematic-drift       |
| $\ConformalQuantileRank = \lceil (\CalibrationExampleCount+1)(1-\ConformalMiscoverageRate) \rceil$                                                                  | Which sorted residual sets a clearance inset with coverage $1-\ConformalMiscoverageRate$, and the fewest residuals that can set one                             | @sec-perception-qualifying-error |

: **Key equations of sensor perception**: The relations that turn a sensor's timing and geometry into travel and spatial error, and set the clearance a consumer holds, with the place each is derived. {#tbl-08-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[36,46,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Spatial perception and age of information"}
* **Observation age begins at capture and is paid in travel:**\index{Perception!observation age}\index{Perception!blind distance} Hardware-latched exposure timestamps, row readout schedules, and bounded clock conversion enable downstream consumers to compute a qualified upper age bound. Every microsecond elapsed from photon arrival to actuator response translates directly into unobserved travel ($\BlindTravelDistance = \SpeedAtDetection \cdot \PrebrakeDelay$) deducted from the physical clearance margin.
* **Choose the measurement for the decision:**\index{Perception!multimodal fusion} Photometric appearance, metric range, Doppler radial velocity, high-rate edge transitions, and tactile contact deformation address distinct physical questions. Multi-sensor fusion improves system resilience only when sensor spatial coverage and correlated common-cause failure modes are rigorously qualified.
* **Fix the geometry before interpreting it:**\index{Hardware!rolling shutter}\index{Perception!calibration drift} Rolling-shutter readout shears geometric edges under vehicle motion ($\FiniteChange \CartesianXCoordinate = \BaseTravelSpeed \cdot \SensorRowIndex \cdot \RollingShutterRowReadout$), requiring per-row pose compensation prior to spatial triangulation. Mechanical vibration and thermal cycling also induce extrinsic calibration drift. An extrinsic shift of `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.theta_ext_str` rad at `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.z_ext_str` projects to `{python} ExtrinsicErrorBudget.dx_ext_str` laterally, as large as the entire localization allowance $\LocalizationBound$. Consequently, every calibration record must carry an explicit validity envelope that consumers verify prior to inference.
* **A wrong timestamp is worse than a lost frame:**\index{Perception!timestamp integrity} A dropped frame is an overt failure that triggering systems can handle gracefully, whereas a plausible but misdated frame silently displaces an obstacle's reconstructed position while reporting deceptively narrow uncertainty. Hardware capture timestamps, clock synchronization error bounds, sequence continuity checks, and age validation must always precede payload interpretation.
* **Claimed error must be measured:**\index{Machine Learning!geometric uncertainty} Softmax classification confidences and depth-bin logits do not characterize spatial tail risk, and zero-mean covariance matrices fail to capture systematic calibration bias. Bounding collision risk requires empirical residual quantiles evaluated against high-precision ground truth across operational conditions to establish defensible clearance insets.
* **The contract bounds what a consumer can refuse:**\index{Perception!observation contract}\index{Perception!silent failure}\index{Perception!dated snapshots} The observation contract packages capture epoch, clock conversion bounds, reference frame, calibration identity, error bounds, and hardware health flags so the planning permission path can reject untrustworthy claims before reading payload data. Even a fully operational sensor can report a clear path that does not exist, and structured observation tokens do not guarantee that downstream policies compensate for transport latency. Establishing semantic truth requires independent cross-modal verification, and spatial memory must synthesize these dated snapshots into a coherent state that persists through occlusion.
:::

Perception supplies the grounded evidence that physical action needs: detected obstacles, identified affordances, and measured range and velocity across complementary modalities. Its output is still a sequence of isolated measurements, each bound to a capture epoch and a sensor frame, and each qualified for the instant it was captured. A qualified measurement states where something was, how old that knowledge is, and how far to trust it. It never states where that thing is now, and when a worker steps behind a rack upright, direct perception falls silent.

The observation contract is where Part III's law, proposal is not permission, first takes physical form. A confident detection does not grant permission to move. The permission path admits motion only on evidence whose age, frame, and error it can check against the clearance that remains, and it refuses everything else before reading the payload. Every later stage in this part inherits that discipline, because each one consumes a dated claim that it did not produce and cannot refresh.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-perception-history}

The geometric foundations of computer vision trace back to photogrammetry and geodesy, where surveyors established rigorous mathematical formulations for optical distortion and perspective projection long before digital processors or mobile robots existed. In the late 1980s, @tsai1987versatile made accurate geometric calibration feasible on off-the-shelf industrial cameras and lenses by developing computationally efficient two-stage optimization algorithms. A decade later, @zhang2000flexible democratized the process by demonstrating that a camera could recover its intrinsic parameters and radial distortion from a planar checkerboard pattern observed at several unconstrained orientations. This formulation transformed camera calibration from an exotic cleanroom procedure into a practical workshop routine. Concurrently, @hartley2003multiple codified the multiple-view projective geometry that underpins stereo disparity, epipolar constraints, and triangulation error. As cameras mounted directly onto robotic manipulators, hand-eye calibration techniques [@shiu1989calibration; @tsai1989new] resolved the rigid kinematic transformations relating camera frames to robot end-effectors. @furgale2013unified generalized this problem to continuous-time systems by integrating temporal delay estimation directly into spatial extrinsics, demonstrating that camera-to-inertial sensor time offsets must be estimated as dynamic parameters rather than assumed to be zero. Together, these developments established an essential systems insight: sensor calibration is never a static constant retrieved from an assembly drawing, but an evolving state estimate bounded by physical drift, mechanical compliance, and thermal expansion.

Sensor hardware diversified along a parallel trajectory as real-time autonomy demanded richer, faster environmental feedback. The autonomous driving competitions of the mid-2000s established scanning laser rangefinders as the primary metric sensor for navigation in unstructured environments [@thrun2006stanley]. Mechanically spinning multi-beam LiDAR systems delivered direct, dense depth measurements, yet their physical rotation introduced significant motion distortion across individual scan lines, which requires per-point timestamping and motion unwinding as detailed in @sec-perception-lidar-age. To overcome the bandwidth and latency limits of synchronous frame-based sensing, neuromorphic engineering [@mead1990] introduced event-based vision sensors featuring independent pixels that emit asynchronous signals only when local log-intensity changes exceed a threshold [@lichtsteiner2008128]. Over the subsequent decade, algorithmic frameworks for event cameras [@gallego2022event] revealed their remarkable microsecond-level temporal resolution and high dynamic range, while also exposing their fundamental limitation: complete blindness to static scenes in the absence of relative motion. Operating high-rate heterogeneous sensors simultaneously required rethinking temporal coordination. Clock synchronization had evolved as a classical problem in distributed computer systems [@lamport1978time], but physical embodiment demanded hardware-level precision. The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol [@ieee15882002; @ieee15882019] addressed this requirement by embedding hardware timestamping directly into the network physical layer, enabling modern LiDARs, cameras, and compute nodes to align their measurement epochs to a shared master clock that real-time safety monitors can verify.

The third pillar of reliable physical perception is the formal qualification of error. Traditional robotic state estimation frequently assumed Gaussian noise models that systematically underestimated the probability of catastrophic tracking failures in complex environments. Conformal prediction [@vovk2005algorithmic] addressed this vulnerability by proving that exchangeable calibration residuals yield distribution-free prediction regions with exact, non-asymptotic coverage guarantees. @angelopoulos2023gentle made these theoretical foundations accessible to systems practitioners, establishing split-conformal methods as practical tools for safety-critical clearance verification. Observation contracts unite these three lineages. Each contract packages recent calibration revisions, formal network synchronization bounds, and empirical residual distributions. Downstream planning controllers and safety monitors can verify these empirical bounds explicitly rather than placing blind trust in raw transducer outputs.

For further reading, six foundational works elaborate on the geometric modeling, hardware timing, and statistical error qualification developed across this chapter:

- @hartley2003multiple is the classic reference for projective geometry, epipolar constraints, and triangulation, providing the theoretical basis for the stereo depth uncertainty relations analyzed in @sec-perception-error-clearance.
- @szeliski2022computer offers an exhaustive survey of computational image formation, camera calibration, and stereo correspondence from the computer vision perspective, detailing the optical aberrations and sensor transduction phenomena underlying @sec-perception-transduction-calibration.
- @zhang2000flexible presents the ubiquitous planar-pattern calibration method, outlining the closed-form solutions and nonlinear refinement procedures that generate the intrinsic calibration records used throughout production pipelines.
- @furgale2013unified demonstrates continuous-time batch state estimation for multi-sensor suites, proving why temporal offsets between cameras and inertial measurement units must be modeled and optimized as explicit unknowns.
- @gallego2022event provides a thorough review of event-based sensing, tracing hardware architectures from analog pixel circuitry to contemporary tracking and SLAM algorithms while outlining the latency-bandwidth trade-offs relevant to high-speed robotic safety.
- @angelopoulos2023gentle serves as a lucid, practical guide to conformal prediction and distribution-free risk control, clearly articulating the exchangeability conditions that physical distribution shifts such as floor wear, rain, or abrupt lighting changes can compromise in real-world deployment.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From sensory photons to spatial memory"}
How long may a dated measurement keep authorizing motion after the scene that produced it goes out of view? Perception answers only for the instant of capture. When the mobile manipulator pivots past a rack upright, the cross aisle leaves the cameras' view, and a worker can step into the corridor that the last frame recorded as clear. @Sec-memory takes the observation contracts this chapter produced and fuses them, each at its own capture epoch, into a state estimate whose uncertainty grows while no new evidence arrives. That growth sets the deadline after which a remembered empty aisle can no longer support motion, and past that deadline the permission path refuses any proposal that relies on it.
:::
